ONC-06.sub: Toxicology → Cytokine Release Syndrome → Treatment by grade
ONC-06.intro: CRS treatment escalates with the grade. Mild disease is supported while infection is excluded. Once the circulation or lungs are involved, IL-6 — the central mediator — is blocked; if that is not enough, steroids are added. Steroids may blunt the CAR-T cells fighting the cancer, so they wait for the more severe or refractory grades.
why: **Grade 1: supportive — antipyretics, fluids, cultures, empirical antibiotics.** The patient is often neutropenic, so fever is treated as possible sepsis.

**Grade 2: tocilizumab (maximum 3 doses); consider ICU.** Hypotension persisting after fluid boluses, without a pressor and with normal oxygen, is grade 2 — the next step is tocilizumab, not steroids, ventilation or adrenaline for ‘anaphylaxis’. Tocilizumab 8 mg/kg IV (maximum 800 mg) usually breaks fever and hypotension within hours; repeat after 8 hours if needed, up to 3 doses in 24 hours. Dexamethasone 10 mg is added if hypotension persists after one or two doses.

**Grade 3: ICU; tocilizumab or siltuximab plus dexamethasone 10–20 mg 6-hourly.** A patient on a vasopressor or high-flow oxygen still gets tocilizumab as the initial cytokine-targeted drug, with dexamethasone alongside; dexamethasone also crosses into the brain, useful because ICANS often accompanies severe CRS.

**Grade 4: anti-IL-6 plus methylprednisolone 1 g pulse; anakinra if refractory.** Survival now outweighs any concern for the anti-tumour effect. Anakinra blocks the IL-1 receptor, a pathway IL-6 blockade does not reach.
mimic: Tocilizumab vs siltuximab
Tocilizumab blocks the receptor (so IL-6 accumulates in the blood); siltuximab binds and removes the cytokine itself.
traps: “Tocilizumab neutralises circulating IL-6” or “inhibits gp130 directly”
It is a humanised antibody to the IL-6 receptor (membrane and soluble); siltuximab binds IL-6, gp130 is downstream and untouched, anakinra blocks IL-1. Only 59% chose ‘blocks IL-6 receptor’.
“Hypotension after immune effector cells despite fluids: high-dose methylprednisolone or adrenaline for anaphylaxis”
This is grade 2 CRS — tocilizumab first; steroids are for refractory or higher grades.
“Fever settled after tocilizumab, so the CRS is over”
Tocilizumab removes fever quickly; follow pressure, oxygen and watch for ICANS.
decode: 12 h after immune effector cells: fever, BP 88/50 after 2 L saline, SpO₂ 95% on air — next step [DocT GT]
Tocilizumab.
CD19 CAR-T, day 3, on norepinephrine, hypoxaemic, cultures negative — initial cytokine therapy [DocT GT]
Tocilizumab.
Mechanism of tocilizumab in CRS [DocT GT]
Blocks the IL-6 receptor.
ONC-06.punch: CRS treatment climbs with the grade: support for 1, IL-6 blockade for 2, add dexamethasone for 3, pulse methylprednisolone and IL-1 blockade for 4 — tocilizumab blocks the receptor, siltuximab the cytokine.

parts.q: Why does serum IL-6 rise after tocilizumab?
parts.a: With the **IL-6 receptor** blocked, IL-6 is no longer taken up and cleared through it, so the blood level **rises** even as signalling stops — the basis of tocilizumab’s failure in ICANS (ONC-07).

fix: Tocilizumab: maximum 3 doses
At most 3 doses in 24 hours and 4 doses in total.

ONC-07.sub: Toxicology → Neurotoxicity (ICANS) → Definition, picture and treatment
ONC-07.intro: A few days after CAR-T infusion, often as the cytokine storm peaks or just after it, some patients develop a brain disorder of their own. Cytokines and activated endothelium make the blood–brain barrier leak, and inflammatory mediators reach the cerebrospinal fluid. Language and handwriting fail first.
why: **Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome.** The neurotoxicity of any therapy that works by activating immune effector cells.
**CAR-T cells and bispecific antibodies.** Both produce the cytokine and endothelial injury behind CRS.
**Tremor, dysgraphia, aphasia, cerebellar signs, encephalopathy, seizures.** A change in handwriting or word-finding may be the first sign (ONC-08).
**Status epilepticus, coma, paresis, cerebral oedema.** Diffuse cerebral oedema can be fulminant and fatal.

**Corticosteroids.** Dexamethasone crosses the blood–brain barrier and suppresses the inflammation inside it. Tocilizumab does not cross: it blocks peripheral IL-6 receptors, so serum IL-6 rises, more IL-6 reaches the CNS, and there the receptors are unblocked — so neurotoxicity can worsen after tocilizumab.
mimic: ICANS vs CRS
CRS is systemic (fever, hypotension, hypoxia) and responds to tocilizumab; ICANS is neurological and responds to steroids. ICANS can occur without CRS.
traps: “Tocilizumab crosses the blood–brain barrier” / “blocks IL-6 centrally” / “IL-6 is trapped peripherally”
The paradox is the reverse: IL-6 rises and increases in the CNS, where tocilizumab cannot follow. 68% got it.
“Give tocilizumab for isolated ICANS”
Use dexamethasone; tocilizumab may worsen it.
decode: 48 h after CAR-T: fever, hypotension, confusion; tocilizumab given, neurotoxicity worsens — mechanism [DocT GT]
IL-6 increased in the CNS.
ICANS without CRS — drug of choice? [pattern]
Dexamethasone.
ONC-07.punch: ICANS is the cytokine storm reaching the brain through a leaky barrier: writing and language fail first, and because tocilizumab cannot follow IL-6 across the barrier — and raises it — steroids are the treatment.

ONC-08.intro: Because writing and language fail early in ICANS, a ten-point bedside screen — the ICE score — tests exactly those functions, several times a day while the patient is at risk. It is one domain of the ICANS grade; the others are consciousness, seizures, motor weakness and cerebral oedema (ONC-09).
why: **Orientation 4 (year, month, city, hospital); naming three objects 3; following a simple command 1; writing a standard sentence 1; counting back from 100 by tens 1.** Orientation tests global encephalopathy, naming expressive aphasia, writing dysgraphia, counting attention. 10 is normal.
**Grade 1: 7–9; grade 2: 3–6; grade 3: 0–2; grade 4: 0, unarousable.** Lower is worse. A score of 0 is grade 4 only when the patient cannot be roused to try.
traps: “A higher ICE score means worse neurotoxicity”
Lower is worse; 10 is normal (ONC-13).
“The ICE score alone gives the ICANS grade”
The grade is the worst of five domains.
decode: ICE score 5 after CAR-T [pattern]
Grade 2 ICANS (if no worse domain).
ONC-08.punch: The ICE score is a ten-point test of the functions ICANS breaks first — orientation, naming, writing and attention — so a lower score means worse neurotoxicity: 7–9 is grade 1, 3–6 grade 2, 0–2 grade 3.

ONC-09.intro: The ICE score covers only cognition, so the ASTCT grade also takes consciousness, seizures, motor weakness and raised intracranial pressure; the worst sets the grade. Treatment escalates with it: observation, then steroids, then ICU care for seizures and oedema.
why: **Grade 1: wakes spontaneously — monitor; imaging, EEG.** EEG looks for non-convulsive seizures; many centres give levetiracetam prophylaxis.
**Grade 2: wakes to voice — consider steroids; lumbar puncture.** Dexamethasone 10 mg IV, repeated if no improvement; LP when safe excludes infection.

**Grade 3: wakes to touch only; any seizure that resolves; focal oedema on imaging — ICU; dexamethasone 10 mg 6-hourly; antiepileptics.** Needing touch to wake puts the airway at risk, and any seizure signals cortical irritation.

**Grade 4: unarousable; prolonged seizure (>5 min); hemiparesis; diffuse oedema, papilloedema — as for grade 3, plus anakinra or cyclophosphamide (experimental); treat raised ICP.** Raised ICP gets the usual measures, and ASCO/NCCN escalate to methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily for 3 days.
traps: “A single brief seizure is grade 2”
Any clinical seizure that resolves is grade 3.
“Focal oedema on imaging is grade 4”
Focal is grade 3; diffuse is grade 4.
decode: ICANS, rousable only to touch [pattern]
Grade 3 — ICU, dexamethasone 10 mg 6-hourly.
ONC-09.punch: ICANS is graded by its worst sign — voice is 2, touch or any seizure or focal oedema is 3, coma, status, hemiparesis or diffuse oedema is 4 — and steroids, ICU care and ICP control escalate in step.

Grade 3
Grade 4
rows: prolonged >5 min, or repeated without recovery

fix: Grade 4 ICANS: as grade 3
Grade 4 needs high-dose methylprednisolone 1 g a day (usually 3 days), not dexamethasone alone (ASCO/NCCN).

ONC-10.sub: Toxicology → Organ Toxicities → General management of immune-related adverse events
ONC-10.intro: An immune-related adverse event is the immune system attacking a normal organ after its brakes have been removed, so treatment follows the logic of autoimmune disease: stop feeding the attack, exclude alternatives, suppress, and come off slowly.
why: **Hold the drug; exclude infection and pre-existing autoimmune disease.** Infection must be excluded first because the treatment is immunosuppression.
**Prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day or equivalent.** For grade 3–4 events; grade 2 usually gets 0.5–1 mg/kg.

**If no response in 5–7 days, add another immunosuppressant: infliximab for colitis; mycophenolate for hepatitis.** Current ASCO/ESMO guidance calls an event steroid-refractory after about 48–72 hours. Infliximab is avoided in hepatitis because it is itself hepatotoxic.
**Taper slowly, over 4 weeks.** Activated T cells persist, so a fast taper flares; prolonged steroids need Pneumocystis prophylaxis.

**After a grade 3 or 4 event, stop the checkpoint inhibitor permanently.** Grade 4 events and any-grade myocarditis mean permanent discontinuation. Endocrine disease is the exception: the gland is replaced with hormone and the drug can usually resume.
traps: “Infliximab for steroid-refractory checkpoint hepatitis”
Infliximab is hepatotoxic; mycophenolate is used.
“Endocrine irAEs need high-dose steroids and permanent discontinuation”
Hormone replacement treats them; the drug can usually be resumed.
decode: Grade 3 colitis on ipilimumab, no response to IV steroids [pattern]
Infliximab (mycophenolate if it were hepatitis).
ONC-10.punch: Treat an irAE like an autoimmune disease you caused: hold the drug, rule out infection, give high-dose steroids, add infliximab or mycophenolate if they fail, taper slowly — and do not rechallenge after a severe event unless the gland can just be replaced.
fix: Steroid-refractory: no response in 5–7 days
Now: no improvement after about 48–72 hours of high-dose steroids (ASCO/ESMO).
Grade 3–4: stop permanently
Permanent for grade 4 and for myocarditis of any grade; after some grade 3 events (e.g. anti-PD-1 colitis) the drug can be restarted once the event settles to grade 1.

ONC-11.sub: Toxicology → Organ Toxicities → Neurological and cardiac toxicities
ONC-11.intro: Neurological and cardiac complications of novel agents are rare but dangerous. Some are autoimmune (checkpoint inhibitors attacking nerve, muscle, meninges or myocardium); some are vascular (drugs raising blood pressure and damaging endothelium); some are allergic (antibodies releasing mast-cell mediators into the coronaries). The mechanism dictates the treatment.
why: **Guillain–Barré, myasthenia: anti-PD-1/PD-L1, sunitinib — IVIG, plasma exchange, steroids.** Checkpoint inhibitors are the main cause. Because the attack is T-cell driven, the checkpoint form gets steroids as well as IVIG or plasma exchange. Myasthenia can overlap with myositis and myocarditis — check troponin and CK.

**PRES: monoclonals, TKIs — stop the drug, control BP.** When pressure exceeds cerebral autoregulation and the endothelium is injured, fluid leaks into the posterior white matter: seizures, headache, cortical blindness, hypertension. The same syndrome follows calcineurin inhibitors (ciclosporin, tacrolimus) after transplant, and the management is identical — withdraw or reduce the trigger and lower the pressure; it usually reverses.
**Aseptic meningitis: monoclonals, checkpoint inhibitors — steroids, IVIG, rituximab.** Lymphocytic CSF; exclude infection before steroids.

**Myocarditis: checkpoint inhibitors — high-dose steroids, IVIG.** T-cell infiltration in the first weeks, with conduction block, arrhythmia and heart failure — the most often fatal irAE. Pulse methylprednisolone early, and the drug is stopped permanently.

**Kounis syndrome: monoclonal antibodies — treat as ACS plus anaphylaxis; morphine with caution.** Mast-cell mediators cause coronary spasm or plaque rupture; morphine releases histamine and can deepen the reaction.

**Acute coronary syndrome: bevacizumab, trastuzumab — treat as ACS.** Bevacizumab damages endothelium and promotes arterial thrombosis. Trastuzumab’s signature is reversible LV systolic dysfunction rather than coronary occlusion; 5-fluorouracil causes coronary vasospasm.
mimic: PRES vs its lookalikes after transplant

Posterior vasogenic oedema with hypertension on a CNI is PRES; it is not a posterior fossa tumour (no decompression), HSV encephalitis (temporal, febrile — aciclovir) or venous sinus thrombosis (anticoagulation).
Checkpoint myocarditis vs ACS
Both raise troponin; myocarditis comes weeks after starting a checkpoint inhibitor, often with conduction block and myositis, and the coronaries are normal.
traps: “Seizures, cortical blindness and posterior oedema on ciclosporin: neurosurgery, aciclovir or anticoagulation”
Withdraw or reduce the calcineurin inhibitor and control BP aggressively.
“Steroids are not used in Guillain–Barré”
True for classical GBS, but checkpoint-related GBS gets steroids too.
“Checkpoint myocarditis is mild and self-limiting”
It is the most often fatal irAE; pulse steroids early, stop the drug permanently.
decode: HSCT recipient on ciclosporin: seizures, hypertension, cortical blindness, posterior white-matter oedema — immediate step [DocT GT]
Withdraw or reduce the calcineurin inhibitor; aggressive BP control.
Ptosis, myalgia and raised troponin 3 weeks after nivolumab [pattern]
Myasthenia–myositis–myocarditis overlap — high-dose steroids.
Chest pain with urticaria during a rituximab infusion [pattern]
Kounis syndrome.
ONC-11.punch: Read each syndrome by its mechanism: autoimmune ones need steroids even when classical teaching says otherwise, vascular ones — PRES from any trigger — need the drug stopped and the pressure lowered, and allergic coronary events need ACS and anaphylaxis care together.

fix: Trastuzumab causes ACS
Trastuzumab causes (usually reversible) left-ventricular dysfunction, not ACS. The ACS drugs are 5-FU/capecitabine (coronary spasm) and bevacizumab (arterial thrombosis).
Checkpoint myocarditis row
Add: stop the checkpoint inhibitor permanently at any grade, and give methylprednisolone 500–1000 mg a day.

ONC-12.sub: Toxicology → Organ Toxicities → Lung, kidney, endocrine and liver
ONC-12.intro: Any organ can be injured by these drugs, and the ICU question is always: drug, cancer, or infection in an immunosuppressed patient? The answer decides whether to give steroids — which help immune toxicity but harm infection.
why: **Pneumonitis: separate infection (Pneumocystis, CMV) from drug (anti-PD-1, rituximab, dasatinib) by CT and bronchoalveolar lavage; then steroids.** Both give ground-glass change; steroids would worsen the infections, so lavage comes first.

**Renal: checkpoint inhibitors — tubulointerstitial nephritis, median onset 3 months; anti-VEGF — thrombotic microangiopathy; rituximab, TKIs — tumour lysis.** T cells infiltrate the interstitium (PPIs and NSAIDs are co-triggers); VEGF loss injures the glomerular endothelium; rapid killing releases uric acid, phosphate and potassium.

**Hypophysitis: anti-CTLA-4 (ipilimumab) — headache, visual disturbance, pituitary failure; MRI and hormone levels; replace hormones.** ACTH deficiency causes secondary adrenal insufficiency — the commonest mechanism of adrenal failure on a checkpoint inhibitor. Give hydrocortisone before thyroxine, because thyroxine speeds cortisol metabolism and can precipitate crisis. Aldosterone is preserved, so there is no hyperkalaemia; replacement is usually lifelong.
**Thyroid: hypo- or hyperthyroidism in 1–10%.** Thyroiditis often passes through a transient thyrotoxic phase to permanent hypothyroidism; more typical of anti-PD-1.
**Hepatitis: 5–10%; from transaminitis to fulminant failure; steroids.** Exclude viral hepatitis and metastases; refractory cases get mycophenolate, not infliximab (ONC-10).
mimic: Hypophysitis vs primary adrenalitis
Hypophysitis: low ACTH, other pituitary hormones low, no hyperkalaemia. Primary adrenal failure (rare with checkpoint inhibitors): high ACTH, hyperkalaemia.
traps: “In hypophysitis replace thyroxine first”
Hydrocortisone first, or thyroxine may precipitate adrenal crisis.
“Start steroids for pneumonitis straight away”
Exclude Pneumocystis and CMV with BAL first.
decode: Headache, fatigue, low sodium, low ACTH and TSH on ipilimumab [pattern]
Hypophysitis — hydrocortisone first, then MRI.
Rising creatinine with sterile pyuria 3 months into pembrolizumab [pattern]
Tubulointerstitial nephritis.
ONC-12.punch: In every organ the first step is to separate drug from infection and cancer, and the treatment follows the mechanism: steroids for immune injury, hormone replacement for a destroyed gland — cortisol before thyroxine — and stopping the drug for vascular injury.

ONC-13.sub: Toxicology → Organ Toxicities → True or false
ONC-13.intro: This card checks the deck’s key distinctions. Each statement turns on one detail met earlier.
why: **False — blinatumomab targets CD3 and CD19.** CD20 is rituximab’s target (ONC-01).
**True — ipilimumab blocks CTLA-4,** the early brake that competes with CD28 for CD80/86 (ONC-02).
**False — fever is required.** Fever ≥38 °C makes it CRS; the grade then comes from blood pressure and oxygen (ONC-05).
**False — positive-pressure ventilation is grade 4.** Grade 3 is high-flow oxygen, face mask or non-rebreather (ONC-05).
**True — tocilizumab blocks the IL-6 receptor;** siltuximab binds IL-6 itself (ONC-06).
**False — a lower ICE score is worse.** It counts tasks done correctly out of 10 (ONC-08).
**True — hypophysitis is typical of anti-CTLA-4 therapy.** Pituitary cells express CTLA-4, so the antibody binds the gland there (ONC-12).
**True — dasatinib is linked to pleural effusion,** exudative and lymphocytic, from off-target kinase inhibition (ONC-03).
traps: “Tocilizumab and siltuximab both bind IL-6”
Only siltuximab binds IL-6; tocilizumab blocks its receptor.
decode: True/false on CRS grading or targets [pattern]
Check fever, number of pressors, positive pressure; match antibody to molecule.
ONC-13.punch: Every statement turns on one detail from the deck — the target of each antibody, fever and positive pressure in CRS grading, receptor versus cytokine for IL-6 blockade, and lower-is-worse for the ICE score.

ARDS-01.intro: Before the definitions, the landmarks that frame them. ARDS was first a bedside description, then a consensus definition revised twice, and all along it has had one histological picture behind it.
why: **Ashbaugh, 1967 (12 patients; Lancet).** Ashbaugh and colleagues described adults with acute tachypnoea, cyanosis refractory to oxygen, stiff lungs and diffuse infiltrates after varied insults — the features that every later definition tried to pin down.

**AECC 1994 → Berlin 2012 → new global definition 2023.** AECC gave the first shared criteria; Berlin fixed its gaps (timing, PEEP, wedge pressure, ALI) — see ARDS-05; the 2023 definition widened it to non-intubated patients and low-resource settings (ARDS-06).

**Diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes.** Hyaline membranes are layers of fibrin and cell debris lining the alveoli, laid down in the exudative stage (ARDS-08). A post-mortem lung at one week shows them.
mimic: Diffuse alveolar damage vs ARDS
DAD is the pathology, ARDS the clinical syndrome; only about half of patients who meet clinical criteria show DAD at autopsy (one criticism of Berlin, ARDS-05).
traps: “Hyaline membranes mark the fibrotic stage”
They are the hallmark of the early exudative stage, within the first week.
decode: [pattern] Histological hallmark of ARDS / post-mortem lung at one week
Diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes.
[pattern] Order of ARDS definitions
AECC 1994, Berlin 2012, global definition 2023.
ARDS-01.punch: ARDS is a clinical syndrome defined by consensus — AECC, Berlin, then the 2023 global definition — and its pathology, when present, is diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes.

ARDS-02.intro: Once ARDS could be graded, LUNG SAFE asked how often it occurs and how well it is treated. It is the study behind the statements that ARDS is common and under-recognised.
why: **459 ICUs, 50 countries, 29,144 patients.** A four-week, prospective snapshot of ICU admissions in the winter of 2014 (Bellani, JAMA 2016) — large enough to give real-world proportions rather than trial figures.
**Mild 30.0%, moderate 46.6%, severe 23.4%.** Moderate is the commonest grade; severe is the smallest group.

**Common (about 10% of ICU admissions, 23% of ventilated patients) and under-recognised and under-treated; hospital mortality about 40%.** Clinicians recognised only about 60% of cases, fewer in mild ARDS, plateau pressure was often not measured, and few patients with severe ARDS were proned. Mortality rose with grade.
mimic: LUNG SAFE mortality vs Berlin mortality
Berlin’s 27/32/45% come from the definition’s own validation cohort (ARDS-04); LUNG SAFE’s overall hospital mortality is about 40%.
traps: “Severe ARDS is the commonest grade”
Moderate is, at 46.6% (ARDS-13d).
decode: [pattern] Commonest Berlin grade in LUNG SAFE
Moderate.
[pattern] Key message of LUNG SAFE
ARDS is common and under-recognised, and lung-protective measures are under-used.
ARDS-02.punch: LUNG SAFE: ARDS affects about one in ten ICU admissions, is mostly moderate, is missed in about 40% of cases, and kills about 40% in hospital.

ARDS-03.intro: This is the definition that every case vignette is checked against. Each of its four criteria answers one question: is it acute, is it both lungs, is it more than heart failure, and how bad is the oxygenation on a standard amount of PEEP?
why: **Within 1 week of a known insult, or of new or worsening respiratory symptoms.** In practice most patients become hypoxic within hours to a day or two of the insult; the one-week window is wide so that almost every case is captured. So a vignette of respiratory failure 3–4 days after pancreatitis or septic shock is well within it.

**Bilateral opacities on chest X-ray or CT, not fully explained by effusion, collapse or nodules.** Unilateral opacity points to pneumonia, collapse or effusion, not ARDS. A CXR with diffuse bilateral alveolar shadowing in a ventilated patient is the textbook image.

**Not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload; if no risk factor is present, an objective test (echo) is needed.** The word is ‘fully’: hydrostatic oedema may coexist, so a raised wedge pressure does not exclude ARDS. When there is a clear risk factor (sepsis, pancreatitis, trauma), the clinical judgement is enough; when there is none, echo must show the heart is not the cause.

**P/F ≤300 on PEEP or CPAP ≥5 cmH₂O.** PEEP recruits collapsed alveoli and raises PaO₂, so a P/F ratio means little unless the PEEP is known; Berlin sets a floor of 5 cmH₂O. The grade within ≤300 is ARDS-04.
mimic: ARDS vs pre-eclamptic pulmonary oedema
Both give bilateral infiltrates in HELLP; a normal LV on echo with P/F 170 and a risk factor makes it ARDS.
ARDS vs amniotic fluid embolism
AFE is a sudden cardiorespiratory collapse during labour or just after delivery, with hypotension and DIC — not hypoxaemia developing with a normal LV, as in this vignette.
traps: “Berlin needs PAWP ≤18 mmHg” or “PAWP >18 completes the definition”
Wedge pressure is not in Berlin; >18 would point towards a cardiac cause, and the required criterion is ‘respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure’.
“Post-partum HELLP with bilateral infiltrates is just pulmonary oedema”
About a fifth of the cohort missed this, and pulmonary oedema is the obvious pull. Once echo shows no LV failure, the oedema is not fully cardiac and the four criteria are met — it is ARDS.
“The 1-week window means symptoms usually appear late”
Most patients are symptomatic within the first day; one week is the outer limit, not the usual time.
decode: Bilateral opacities, P/F 180 on PEEP 6 after pancreatitis — which further finding is needed? [DocT GT]
Respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload.
Post-partum HELLP, P/F 170, bilateral infiltrates, normal LV on echo — diagnosis? [DocT GT]
ARDS: all four criteria are met.
Ventilated patient, diffuse bilateral shadowing on CXR — diagnosis? [DocT QBank]
ARDS.
After an injury, when do ARDS symptoms usually begin? [Marrow]
Within 24 hours (the Berlin limit is 1 week).
ARDS-03.punch: Berlin asks four things — within a week, both lungs, not fully cardiac, and P/F ≤300 on PEEP ≥5; no wedge pressure is needed, and a normal echo is required only when there is no risk factor.

parts.q: After an insult, when do ARDS symptoms usually begin?
parts.a: **Usually within 24 hours** (Marrow key); the Berlin window of 1 week is the limit that captures almost all cases.

ARDS-04.intro: Once the four criteria are met, the P/F ratio on PEEP ≥5 sets the grade. The grade is asked directly, inside an ABG you must calculate yourself, and as the gate for non-invasive support.
why: **Mild 201–300, moderate 101–200, severe ≤100 (all on PEEP ≥5).** Each band includes its upper limit: 300 is mild, 200 is moderate, 100 is severe. Always calculate P/F from the FiO₂ given — PaO₂ 58 on FiO₂ 0.75 is 77, severe, however unremarkable 58 looks.
**Mortality 27%, 32% and 45%.** These are the figures from Berlin’s validation cohort; the step from moderate to severe is the largest.

**Mild only: non-invasive CPAP may satisfy the PEEP criterion; moderate and severe need invasive ventilation in the original Berlin wording.** A non-invasive mask leaks and gives an unreliable FiO₂ and PEEP, so Berlin accepted it only at the mildest end. That is also where a trial of NIV is reasonable; in moderate–severe ARDS, shock or refractory hypoxaemia, NIV often fails and the delayed intubation is associated with higher mortality (in LUNG SAFE, NIV was linked to higher ICU mortality when P/F was below 150). A HACOR score >5 after one hour of NIV predicts failure.
mimic: Severe hypoxaemia vs the acid–base disorder in the same ABG
pH 7.295, PaCO₂ 63, HCO₃⁻ 29.8 is a partly compensated respiratory acidosis, but P/F 77 is the dominant and life-threatening finding.
traps: “The ABG shows a compensated respiratory acidosis” (only 37% of the cohort got this right)

There is a respiratory acidosis with partial metabolic compensation — pH is still low, so it is not fully compensated — but the question is about ARDS, and P/F 58/0.75 = 77 is severe hypoxaemia. DocT’s explanation that the gas shows ‘no acid–base disturbance’ is wrong; the key (severe hypoxaemia) is still the best answer.
“P/F 100–200 is severe”
100–200 is moderate; severe is ≤100. This is the NEET 2024 recall.
“NIV suits moderate ARDS with distress” or “refractory severe ARDS”
NIV is reasonable only in mild ARDS without contraindications. Note that the keyed option calls P/F 200 ‘mild’; by Berlin, 200 is moderate — the option is still the best of the four.
decode: Septic shock, bilateral opacities, echo normal, P/F 180 on PEEP 8 — severity? [DocT GT]
Moderate (101–200).
COVID ARDS, ABG shown — interpretation? [DocT QBank, DocT GT]
Calculate PaO₂/FiO₂ from the FiO₂ on the slip; 77 = severe hypoxaemia.
Which does NOT satisfy severe ARDS? [NEET 2024, DocT GT]
P/F 100–200 (that is moderate).
When is NIPPV appropriate in ARDS? [DocT QBank]
Mild ARDS with no contraindications.
ARDS-04.punch: Grade on PEEP ≥5: >200 to 300 mild, >100 to 200 moderate, ≤100 severe — calculate P/F from the FiO₂ in the stem, and keep NIV for mild ARDS only.

fix: WATCH: PEEP below 5 and not on HFNO

Two definitions are mixed here. Berlin 2012 needs invasive ventilation or CPAP/NIV with PEEP ≥5 (CPAP allowed for mild only) and never accepts HFNO; the 2023 global definition accepts HFNO ≥30 L/min, but does not grade non-intubated patients.

ARDS-05.intro: Berlin was written to fix the AECC definition, so each change answers a known flaw. The examiners’ favourite is the wedge pressure, because old keys still use it.
why: **AECC: ‘acute’ undefined, P/F ≤300 = ALI and ≤200 = ARDS, PEEP not considered, PAOP ≤18 mmHg, bilateral infiltrates on X-ray, no risk factor. Berlin: within 1 week, ALI removed (now mild ARDS), three P/F grades, PEEP ≥5 required, wedge removed, X-ray or CT with exclusions, risk factor included.** The wedge was dropped because pulmonary artery catheters are rarely used and because hydrostatic and permeability oedema often coexist — a PAOP above 18 does not exclude ARDS, and one below 18 does not prove it. PEEP was added because the same patient’s P/F changes with it.

**Remaining criticisms: PEEP level and ventilator settings not standardised, no set timing for the gas; needs PEEP, ABG and imaging (unusable in low-resource settings); P/F varies with PEEP and FiO₂; poor X-ray agreement between readers; weak correlation with diffuse alveolar damage at autopsy.** The resource and blood-gas problems are what the 2023 global definition answers (ARDS-06).
mimic: ARDS vs cardiogenic pulmonary oedema
Under Berlin, they are separated by the clinical picture and echo, not by a wedge cut-off.
traps: “A wedge above 18 mmHg rules out ARDS”

That is AECC thinking. Under Berlin the wedge is gone and a raised PAOP can coexist with ARDS (ARDS-03 watch). A low wedge (Marrow’s keyed 16 mmHg) still favours non-cardiogenic oedema, so pick it when it is offered — it supports ARDS, it does not define it.
“ALI is a Berlin category”
It was renamed mild ARDS (ARDS-13c).
decode: Which finding separates ARDS from cardiogenic pulmonary oedema? [Marrow]
Keyed PCWP 16 mmHg (below the AECC 18): a low wedge favours non-cardiogenic oedema; Berlin itself uses echo and clinical judgement instead.
[pattern] Which AECC feature did Berlin remove?
Wedge pressure ≤18 and the term ALI.
ARDS-05.punch: Berlin fixed AECC by defining ‘acute’ as one week, adding PEEP ≥5, grading severity, and dropping both the wedge pressure and ‘ALI’ — so a wedge cut-off answer is AECC thinking.

ARDS-06.intro: Berlin needed a ventilator, a blood gas and an X-ray, so it missed patients on high-flow oxygen and most patients in low-resource settings. The 2023 global definition keeps Berlin’s core and adds ways in.
why: **Non-intubated patients are included if on HFNO ≥30 L/min or NIV/CPAP with ≥5 cmH₂O.** High-flow oxygen became the common support for hypoxaemic patients during COVID-19, and Berlin could not count them. Non-intubated patients are not graded by severity.
**SpO₂/FiO₂ ≤315, valid only when SpO₂ is ≤97%.** Above 97% the oxyhaemoglobin curve is flat, so SpO₂ no longer tracks PaO₂ and the ratio is meaningless.
**Lung ultrasound is accepted for bilateral opacities** (performed by a trained operator), which brings imaging to the bedside where X-ray or CT is not available.

**No PEEP, flow or device requirement in resource-limited settings (follows the Kigali modification).** In Kigali, a definition using S/F and ultrasound, without PEEP, identified ARDS where blood gases and ventilators were scarce.
mimic: P/F vs S/F cut-offs
traps: “The 2023 definition changed the P/F cut-offs”
They are unchanged at 300, 200, 100.
“S/F can be used at any saturation”
Only when SpO₂ ≤97%.
decode: [pattern] Patient on HFNO 40 L/min with bilateral opacities — ARDS by which definition?
The 2023 global definition, not Berlin.
[pattern] S/F threshold for ARDS
≤315, with SpO₂ ≤97%.
ARDS-06.punch: The 2023 definition keeps Berlin’s cut-offs but admits HFNO ≥30 L/min, S/F ≤315 (SpO₂ ≤97%) and lung ultrasound, and drops PEEP and device requirements where resources are limited.

ARDS-07.intro: The story starts with the insult. The lung can be injured from the airway side, damaging the alveolar epithelium first, or from the blood side, where circulating inflammatory mediators damage the capillary endothelium first. That side of entry is the whole basis of the direct/indirect split.
why: **Direct: pneumonia, aspiration of gastric contents, lung contusion, inhalational injury, near-drowning, pulmonary vasculitis, transfusion (TRALI). Indirect: non-pulmonary sepsis, major trauma, pancreatitis, severe burns, non-cardiogenic shock, drug overdose.** Ask whether the injury reached the lung through the airway or the lung itself (direct) or through the blood (indirect). Pancreatitis injures the lung through circulating enzymes and cytokines, so it is indirect; aspiration, pneumonia and smoke reach the alveoli through the airway, so they are direct. Most sources place transfusion (TRALI) with the indirect causes, because antibodies in donor plasma reach the lung through the blood.

**Pneumonia and sepsis are the commonest causes (then aspiration).** In LUNG SAFE, pneumonia accounted for well over half of cases. The more severe the illness, the higher the risk: trauma patients with APACHE II ≥16 have about 2.5 times the risk, and the commonest causes in trauma are lung contusion, multiple fractures and chest-wall trauma (Harrison’s).
mimic: Pulmonary contusion vs major trauma
Contusion is a direct cause (the lung is struck); trauma without lung injury is indirect, through shock and transfusion.
Severe burns vs inhalational injury
The burn itself is indirect; smoke reaching the airway is direct.
traps: “Inhalational injury is an indirect cause”
Smoke reaches the alveoli through the airway, so it is direct; the burn of the skin is indirect.
“The first danger in a burn with bronchial blisters is ARDS”
The immediate complication is laryngeal oedema; pneumonia and ARDS come at about 4–5 days, and subglottic stenosis, bronchiectasis and bronchiolitis obliterans later.
decode: Which is an indirect cause of ARDS? [DocT GT]
Acute pancreatitis (aspiration, pneumonia and inhalation are direct).
Burn with bronchial blisters — immediate complication of inhalation injury? [Marrow]
Laryngeal oedema.
APACHE II score that raises ARDS risk 2.5-fold in trauma? [Marrow]
ARDS-07.punch: Direct causes reach the alveolus through the airway, indirect ones through the blood; pneumonia and sepsis lead the list, and pancreatitis is the classic indirect cause.

parts.q: Inhalation injury: timeline of complications?
parts.a: **Immediate: laryngeal oedema**; at about 4–5 days: pneumonia and ARDS; late: subglottic stenosis, bronchiectasis, bronchiolitis obliterans (Marrow).

fix: Transfusion (TRALI) listed as a direct cause
Standard sources (Ware & Matthay; the Berlin risk-factor list) put transfusion with the indirect causes: the injury reaches the lung through the blood.

ARDS-08.intro: After the insult, the lung goes through a sequence of injury, attempted repair and, in some patients, scarring. The stage explains what you see at the bedside: flooding early, stiff lungs with dead space and pulmonary hypertension late.
why: **Exudative (first 7 days), proliferative (from about 7–10 days), fibrotic (after 10–14 days).** These are your notes’ timings; other texts give proliferative as days 7–21 and fibrotic after 3 weeks. The stages overlap, and many patients recover after the proliferative stage without fibrosis.

**Exudative: type I cell and endothelial injury, protein-rich oedema, neutrophils, hyaline membranes. Proliferative: type II pneumocyte hyperplasia, fibroblasts, oedema organises. Fibrotic: collagen, obliterated architecture, pulmonary hypertension.** Type I cells cover the alveolus and die easily; type II cells are the progenitors that multiply to re-line it, so their hyperplasia is a sign of repair. When repair fails, fibrosis (fibrosing alveolitis) replaces alveoli and capillaries: compliance falls further, dead space rises, the pulmonary vascular bed is lost and pulmonary hypertension follows, with a risk of pneumothorax.
mimic: Fibrotic ARDS vs organising pneumonia

Organising pneumonia is a separate entity with plugs of granulation tissue, patchy consolidation and a brisk steroid response; two weeks of ventilation with falling compliance, dead space, pulmonary hypertension and linear opacities is ARDS going fibrotic.
Fibrotic ARDS vs pulmonary embolism
PE raises dead space and pulmonary pressures, but does not lower compliance or give linear opacities.
traps: “Organising pneumonia” or “bronchiolitis obliterans” for the two-week ventilator-dependent patient
31% missed this. The combination of low compliance, high dead space, new pulmonary hypertension and linear opacities after two weeks is the fibrotic stage — fibrosing alveolitis.
“Type II pneumocytes proliferate in the fibrotic stage”
They proliferate in the proliferative stage (ARDS-13f).
decode: ARDS, ventilator-dependent at 2 weeks, low compliance, high dead space, new pulmonary hypertension, linear opacities — pathology? [DocT GT]
Fibrosing alveolitis (fibrotic stage).
COVID on MV, died at 1 week — post-mortem lung? [Marrow]
Thick fibrin layer lining alveoli: hyaline membranes (exudative stage).
ARDS-08.punch: Exudative oedema with hyaline membranes in week one, type II cell repair after it, and in some a fibrotic stage that brings low compliance, dead space and pulmonary hypertension.

ARDS-09.intro: Each bedside feature of ARDS follows from one event: the alveolar–capillary barrier leaks. Fluid and protein flood the alveoli, the flooded units stay perfused, and the lung left over is small. The questions test whether you can name the mechanism behind each sign.
why: **Increased permeability of the alveolar–capillary barrier, not raised hydrostatic pressure.** Injured endothelium and epithelium let protein through, so the oedema fluid is rich in protein, close to plasma. In cardiogenic oedema the barrier is intact and a high capillary pressure (PCWP 24 in the vignette) pushes out a protein-poor transudate — the mechanism keyed in the heart-failure question.

**Shunt: flooded and collapsed alveoli are perfused but not ventilated.** Blood through those units never meets the inspired gas, however much oxygen is given; and blood leaving the healthy units is already nearly saturated, so it cannot carry extra to make up. With a large shunt, PaO₂ barely rises on 100% oxygen. In V/Q mismatch, low-ventilation units still receive some gas, so extra oxygen does correct them. PEEP, by re-opening alveoli, is what reduces shunt.
**Loss of aerated lung and surfactant dysfunction.** Fewer open alveoli means each breath goes into a smaller lung (ARDS-10), and damaged surfactant raises surface tension so alveoli collapse.

**Microvascular thrombosis and over-distension of the remaining aerated units; a high dead-space fraction predicts mortality.** Clots in capillaries leave ventilated alveoli unperfused, and over-stretched alveoli compress their own capillaries. Both waste ventilation, PaCO₂ rises, and the dead-space fraction is an independent predictor of death.
mimic: Permeability vs hydrostatic oedema
ARDS: protein-rich exudate, normal heart. Heart failure: protein-poor transudate, raised wedge, Kerley B lines, cardiomegaly.
traps: “Hypoxaemia unresponsive to 100% oxygen in pneumonia is V/Q mismatch” (only half the cohort chose shunt)
Failure to respond to oxygen is the signature of shunt. V/Q mismatch improves with oxygen.
“ARDS hypoxaemia is mainly V/Q mismatch”

It is mainly shunt. One DocT question keys V/Q mismatch only because shunt is not offered — shunt is the extreme end of V/Q mismatch (V/Q of zero), so that key is defensible; choose shunt whenever it is an option.
decode: Severe pneumonia, hypoxaemia unresponsive to 100% oxygen — mechanism? [DocT GT]
Shunt physiology.
Ventilated multilobar pneumonia, persistent hypoxaemia — mechanism? [Marrow]
Shunt: perfused, unventilated alveoli.
ARDS, PaO₂ 52 on FiO₂ 0.6, options without shunt [DocT GT]
V/Q mismatch as the nearest answer.
Heart failure, PCWP 24 — why pulmonary oedema? [DocT GT]
Raised hydrostatic pressure, not increased permeability.
ARDS-09.punch: A leaky barrier gives protein-rich oedema; perfused but flooded alveoli give shunt that oxygen cannot fix; fewer open alveoli lower compliance; and clotted, over-stretched units raise dead space, which predicts death.

ARDS-10.intro: The loss of aerated lung from ARDS-09 has a consequence for every breath you set. CT showed that the ARDS lung is not uniformly stiff: it is a small lung that still works, sitting on top of flooded, collapsed lung.
why: **Gattinoni (CT studies).** CT of ARDS lungs showed dense collapse in the dependent regions and near-normal aeration in a small non-dependent region.

**The ARDS lung is small, not stiff: only a small non-dependent portion stays aerated, the size of a child’s lung.** The ventilated lung of an adult with severe ARDS may be as small as a young child’s.
**Compliance reflects the volume of aerated lung; the aerated part has near-normal compliance.** A low respiratory compliance means fewer open alveoli, not stiffer ones.

**A normal tidal volume over-distends the baby lung, hence low tidal volume and driving-pressure limits.** 500 mL into a lung the size of a child’s stretches it injuriously; tidal volume is set at 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, and driving pressure (tidal volume divided by compliance) measures how large the breath is relative to the lung that is open.
mimic: Baby lung vs sponge lung

The baby lung is functional, not anatomical: the oedematous lung is heavy, and its own weight collapses the dependent parts, so the aerated region moves when the patient is turned — the reason proning helps.
traps: “The ARDS lung is uniformly stiff”
It is small, not stiff (ARDS-13g).
decode: [pattern] Who described the baby lung, and what does compliance reflect?
Gattinoni; the volume of aerated lung.
[pattern] Why low tidal volume in ARDS?
A normal tidal volume over-distends the small aerated lung.
ARDS-10.punch: The ARDS lung is small, not stiff: compliance measures how much lung is open, so tidal volume must be scaled to that small lung.

ARDS-11.intro: Berlin is a syndrome definition, so anything that fills both lungs with fluid, blood, cells or protein in under a week can meet it. The mimics matter because their treatment is different — steroids, plasma exchange, lavage — and the bronchoalveolar lavage is usually what tells them apart.
why: **Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema; diffuse alveolar haemorrhage; acute eosinophilic pneumonia; acute interstitial pneumonia (Hamman–Rich); cryptogenic organising pneumonia; acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis; drug-induced lung disease; lymphangitic carcinomatosis.** Each gives acute bilateral opacities and hypoxaemia, so each can pass all four Berlin criteria, especially when there is no clear risk factor.

**Echo and BNP (cardiac cause); CT chest; bronchoalveolar lavage (eosinophils, haemosiderin-laden macrophages, organisms, malignant cells); lung biopsy rarely.** In diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, the lavage becomes more bloody with each aliquot and shows >20% haemosiderin-laden macrophages; the next step is the systemic cause — ANCA vasculitis, anti-GBM disease, SLE or antiphospholipid syndrome. In acute eosinophilic pneumonia, BAL eosinophils are >25%, typically in a young man who has recently started smoking, with negative cultures; IV methylprednisolone works within 12–48 h. In pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, the lavage is milky with PAS-positive lipoproteinaceous material and CT shows crazy paving; it is treated by whole-lung lavage (± inhaled GM-CSF).

**Trauma-related ARDS: better survival. Pulmonary vs extrapulmonary: similar. Hyperinflammatory phenotype: worse than hypoinflammatory. COVID-19 ARDS: similar mortality, longer ventilation and stay.** The hyperinflammatory phenotype has higher inflammatory markers (IL-6, IL-8), more shock and lower bicarbonate. Trauma patients are usually younger and have a reversible insult.
mimic: Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage vs alveolar proteinosis
Haemosiderin-laden macrophages vs PAS-positive material.
Polyarteritis nodosa vs ANCA vasculitis
PAN is a medium-vessel vasculitis that spares the lung; the small-vessel ANCA vasculitides cause capillaritis and DAH.
traps: “PAN on prednisone explains the alveolar haemorrhage” or “aspirin explains it” (59% wrong)
PAN spares the lung, and low-dose aspirin alone does not cause DAH. Three first-trimester miscarriages point to antiphospholipid syndrome, a recognised cause of DAH.
“PAS-positive lavage is diffuse alveolar haemorrhage”
PAS-positive material is alveolar proteinosis; DAH shows haemosiderin-laden macrophages.
“A new smoker with BAL eosinophils 35% needs antibiotics or ECMO first”
This is acute eosinophilic pneumonia: IV methylprednisolone.
decode: Intubated, bilateral GGO, haemorrhagic secretions, BAL >50% haemosiderin-laden macrophages — which history supports it? [DocT GT]
Three first-trimester miscarriages (antiphospholipid syndrome).
Bilateral infiltrates, BAL PAS-positive material — which ARDS mimic? [DocT GT]
Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis.
Young recent smoker, ARDS picture, BAL eosinophils 35% — next step? [Marrow]
IV methylprednisolone.
ARDS-11.punch: When Berlin criteria are met without a clear risk factor, look for a mimic — and the lavage usually names it: blood for DAH, eosinophils for eosinophilic pneumonia, PAS-positive material for proteinosis.

ARDS-12.intro: COVID-19 tested the ideas of ARDS-09 and ARDS-10. In the early phase some patients were deeply hypoxaemic with fairly normal compliance, which pointed to a vascular problem rather than flooding alone.
why: **Often relatively preserved compliance despite severe hypoxaemia in the early phase.** Much of the hypoxaemia came from perfusion going to poorly ventilated lung rather than from loss of aerated volume. Gattinoni proposed two types: L (low elastance, so near-normal compliance; low lung weight; little to recruit) and H (high elastance, heavy lung, large shunt, recruitable). Larger cohorts (Grasselli, Lombardy; Ferrando, Spain; both 2020) then found compliance in ventilated COVID ARDS spread over the same wide range as classical ARDS, with no separate groups, and no trial has tested ventilation guided by L or H.

**Prominent endothelial injury and microthrombosis; hypoxaemia from loss of hypoxic vasoconstriction.** Normally, vessels to poorly ventilated alveoli constrict and send blood elsewhere; when that reflex is lost, blood keeps flowing through poorly ventilated lung.

**RECOVERY: dexamethasone 6 mg for 10 days lowered 28-day mortality in patients on oxygen or ventilation.** The dose was 6 mg once daily for up to 10 days (or until discharge). The largest benefit was in ventilated patients; there was no benefit in patients not on oxygen.
mimic: COVID vs classical ARDS
Mortality is similar; ventilation and stay are longer in COVID (ARDS-11c).
traps: “COVID ARDS needs a different ventilation strategy”
Ventilation is the same: low tidal volume and proning, as for any ARDS.
“Type L COVID ARDS should be ventilated with larger tidal volumes”
This was proposed from the L/H model, but compliance did not split into two groups in large cohorts and no trial supports it; standard lung-protective ventilation applies.
decode: [pattern] Steroid with mortality benefit in COVID-19 on oxygen or ventilation
Dexamethasone 6 mg for 10 days (RECOVERY).
[pattern] COVID pneumonia, severe hypoxaemia, near-normal compliance, little recruitability — which type?
Type L in Gattinoni’s model; type H is low compliance, heavy lung and recruitable. Large cohorts did not confirm two separate groups.
ARDS-12.punch: Early COVID ARDS may keep near-normal compliance because its hypoxaemia is partly vascular, but it is ventilated like any ARDS, and dexamethasone helps those on oxygen or ventilation.

ARDS-13.sub: Respiratory → ARDS → Revision: true or false
ARDS-13.intro: A sweep through the deck. Each statement turns on one detail from an earlier card.
why: **False — PAOP ≤18 was AECC.** Berlin removed the wedge pressure (ARDS-05).
**True — P/F 200 on PEEP 5 is moderate (101–200).** Each band includes its upper limit (ARDS-04).
**False — ALI was removed; it is now mild ARDS** (ARDS-05).
**False — moderate is the commonest grade in LUNG SAFE, 46.6%** (ARDS-02).
**True — hyaline membranes belong to the exudative stage, the hallmark of diffuse alveolar damage** (ARDS-08).
**False — type II pneumocytes proliferate in the proliferative stage** (ARDS-08).
**False — the ARDS lung is small, not stiff (baby lung)** (ARDS-10).
traps: “P/F 200 is mild”
Exactly 200 is moderate; exactly 300 is mild; exactly 100 is severe.
decode: [pattern] Statements about Berlin vs AECC
Wedge pressure and ALI belong to AECC only.
[pattern] Statements about pathology stages
Hyaline membranes early, type II hyperplasia next, collagen last.
ARDS-13.punch: Most errors on ARDS statements come from AECC leftovers (wedge, ALI), band edges (200 is moderate) and stage order (membranes, then type II cells, then fibrosis).

spine: Insults that injure the lung
ARDS follows a direct insult to the alveolar epithelium, such as pneumonia or aspiration, or an indirect one reaching the lung through the blood, such as sepsis or pancreatitis.
Diffuse alveolar damage in stages
The injured lung passes from exudative oedema with hyaline membranes, through type II cell proliferation, to fibrosis in some patients.
Leaky barrier, shunt, small lung
Protein-rich oedema floods alveoli that stay perfused, so hypoxaemia is from shunt and resists oxygen, and the lung left aerated is small rather than stiff.
Defining it: AECC to Berlin
Berlin defines ARDS by four criteria — onset within a week, bilateral opacities, oedema not fully cardiac, and P/F ≤300 on PEEP ≥5 — and dropped the wedge pressure and the term ALI.
Grading, global reach and burden

P/F grades it mild, moderate or severe; the 2023 definition stretches it to non-intubated patients and settings without blood gases; LUNG SAFE shows it is common, mostly moderate and under-recognised.
Mimics, prognosis and review
Several conditions meet Berlin criteria without being ARDS, and BAL, echo and CT separate them — which matters because some respond to steroids.
RESP01A.primer: The P/F ratio is arterial PO₂ in mmHg divided by FiO₂ as a fraction (PaO₂ 60 on FiO₂ 0.5 gives 120); the lower it is, the worse the oxygenation, and it is only comparable when PEEP is stated. PEEP is the pressure held in the airways at the end of expiration; it keeps collapsed alveoli open, so it changes the P/F ratio. Shunt means blood flowing past alveoli that receive no gas at all, whereas V/Q mismatch means alveoli that are ventilated, but too little for their blood flow — extra oxygen corrects the second, not the first. Compliance is the change in lung volume per unit of pressure; a low value means each breath needs more pressure.

ARDS-14.intro: The story starts before the tube. A patient with acute hypoxaemic failure, often early ARDS, can be given standard oxygen, high-flow nasal oxygen or NIV, and FLORALI is the trial that compared all three. The exam asks it two ways: what the trial showed, and what HFNC actually does to the patient’s breathing.
why: **HFNC vs standard oxygen (face mask) vs NIV, in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure.** Frat and colleagues (NEJM 2015) randomised 310 non-hypercapnic patients with P/F ≤300, most with pneumonia; the NIV arm received HFNC between NIV sessions.

**Intubation at 28 days: no significant difference overall.** The rates were 38% with HFNC, 47% with standard oxygen and 50% with NIV — a trend, not a significant result, so ‘HFNC reduces intubation’ is not what the primary outcome showed.

**Lower 90-day mortality with HFNC; fewer intubations in the subgroup with P/F ≤200.** Neither is the primary outcome: 90-day mortality was a secondary outcome, and the P/F ≤200 intubation result came from a post hoc analysis, so both generate hypotheses rather than prove benefit. The hazard of death at 90 days was about twice as high with standard oxygen (HR 2.01) and two and a half times as high with NIV (HR 2.50), compared with HFNC. NIV did worst; its patients took large tidal volumes, which links this card to P-SILI (ARDS-17). Current ERS (2022) and ESICM (2023) guidance favour HFNC over conventional oxygen in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure.

**FiO₂ 21–100%; washes out anatomical dead space; lowers work of breathing; gives a few cmH₂O of PEEP.** A flow of up to 60 L/min matches or exceeds the patient’s own peak inspiratory flow, so room air is not entrained and the set FiO₂ is the FiO₂ delivered — something no face mask achieves. The flow flushes CO₂ from the nasopharynx, so each breath carries less dead space; the respiratory rate and work of breathing fall, while tidal volume stays the same or rises. Heated, humidified gas is comfortable and keeps secretions moving. The PEEP is small — about 1 cmH₂O per 10 L/min with the mouth closed, less with it open — and it is neither set nor measured. Even so, among the common oxygen devices it is the only one that generates any end-expiratory pressure.
mimic: HFNC vs CPAP/NIV
CPAP and NIV set and hold a known pressure through a sealed mask; HFNC gives only a small, variable pressure through open prongs, but is far better tolerated.
‘High-frequency nasal insufflation’ vs HFNC
There is no distinct standard therapy by that name; the keyed answer simply describes HFNC — high flow, CO₂ washout, mild positive pressure.
traps: “HFNC reduces tidal volume”
It lowers the respiratory rate and work of breathing, but tidal volume is unchanged or larger; this is the false option in ‘all except’ questions.
“HFNC delivers higher pressures than CPAP” or “is CPAP”

Its PEEP is a few cmH₂O at most and falls with an open mouth. The DocT key ‘positive pressure to maintain airway patency’ (only 60% got it right) overstates this; it is still the best of its options, but the leading mechanisms are a reliable FiO₂ and dead-space washout.
“The elderly patient pulling off her mask needs a non-rebreather, mask CPAP or intubation” (only 43% got this right)

She is hypoxaemic but with a normal pH and PaCO₂, and she will not tolerate a mask: HFNC is tolerated through the nose and gives a reliable FiO₂. A non-rebreather is still a mask with an unreliable FiO₂; mask CPAP needs a cooperative patient.
“In FLORALI, HFNC lowered intubation”
Overall it did not (primary outcome negative); only the P/F ≤200 subgroup, in a post hoc analysis, showed fewer intubations.
decode: Which oxygen device can generate PEEP? [NEET 2025]
HFNO — not a non-rebreather, Venturi or Hudson mask.
Benefits of HFNC include all EXCEPT [DocT GT]
Reduce tidal volume.
Primary benefit of HFNO in ARDS [DocT QBank, three versions]

High flow with mild positive pressure, better oxygenation and less work of breathing — the option that does not claim CPAP-level pressure or a fixed tidal volume. Some stems put HFNO on an already ventilated patient; ignore that and answer the mechanism.
Elderly, confused, rib fractures, SpO₂ 89% on 8 L face mask, pulling it off — next step? [DocT GT]
Heated, humidified HFNC.
ARDS-14.punch: FLORALI’s primary outcome was negative, but HFNC was associated with lower 90-day mortality and fewer intubations when P/F was ≤200; it works mainly through a reliable FiO₂, dead-space washout and comfort, with only a little PEEP.

ARDS-15.intro: Once a patient is on HFNC, the danger is staying on it too long while failing. The ROX index puts oxygenation and breathing effort into one bedside number, so failure is seen in hours rather than at the point of collapse.
why: **(SpO₂ ÷ FiO₂) ÷ respiratory rate.** SpO₂ in %, FiO₂ as a fraction. Better oxygenation raises the top line, faster breathing lowers the whole, so the rate must be the divisor — SpO₂ 92% on FiO₂ 0.5 at 30/min gives 184 ÷ 30 = 6.1. It uses SpO₂, not PaO₂, because it is meant to need no blood gas.
**≥4.88 at 2, 6 or 12 h: low risk of intubation.** Roca and colleagues derived it in pneumonia patients on HFNC and validated it in 2019.

**Failure if below 2.85 at 2 h, 3.47 at 6 h, 3.85 at 12 h.** The failure cut-off rises with time, because a patient still struggling after 12 hours has less excuse. Values between the failure cut-off and 4.88 are indeterminate, so the score is repeated.
mimic: ROX vs HACOR
ROX is for HFNC and a lower value is worse; HACOR is for NIV and a higher value is worse (ARDS-16).
traps: “ROX = PaO₂/FiO₂ × RR” or “SpO₂ × RR / FiO₂” (69–83% got the formula right)
ROX uses SpO₂, not PaO₂, and the respiratory rate divides: a faster rate must lower the score.
“A higher ROX predicts failure”
A lower ROX is worse.
decode: Pneumonia on HFNC — correct formula for the ROX index? [DocT GT, three tests]
SpO₂/FiO₂ ÷ RR.
[pattern] ROX 3.2 at 6 h on HFNC — what next?
Below 3.47: high risk of failure, so prepare to intubate rather than wait.
ARDS-15.punch: ROX is SpO₂/FiO₂ divided by the respiratory rate; ≥4.88 predicts HFNC success, and values below 2.85, 3.47 and 3.85 at 2, 6 and 12 h predict failure.

ARDS-16.intro: HACOR does for NIV what ROX does for HFNC. NIV failure in hypoxaemic patients is common, and the harm lies in the delay, so the score is taken after the first hour.
why: **NIV failure in hypoxaemic respiratory failure.** Duan and colleagues (2017) built it from bedside variables to predict who will need intubation.

**Heart rate, acidosis (pH), consciousness (GCS), oxygenation (P/F), respiratory rate; consciousness carries the most points.** A falling GCS weighs most because a drowsy patient cannot protect his airway or cooperate with a mask: of a maximum 25 points, GCS ≤10 scores 10 on its own, more than the worst P/F (6), pH (4) or rate (4).

**>5 at 1 hour of NIV: failure rate above 80%; intubate early.** In the derivation study, among patients with a score above 5 at 1 h who failed NIV, those intubated within 12 hours had lower hospital mortality than those intubated later (66% vs 79%) — an association, but it is the reason the score is used.
mimic: HACOR vs ROX
HACOR: NIV, needs a blood gas, higher is worse. ROX: HFNC, no blood gas, lower is worse.
traps: “NIV suits moderate ARDS with distress, severe ARDS or shock”
NIV is reasonable only in mild ARDS without contraindications (ARDS-04c). The keyed option calls P/F 200 ‘mild’; by Berlin it is moderate — the option is still the best of the four.
decode: Most appropriate scenario for NIPPV in ARDS [DocT QBank]
Mild ARDS with no contraindications to NIPPV (83% got this right).
[pattern] HACOR 7 after 1 h of NIV — next step?
Intubate early: >5 at 1 h predicts failure.
ARDS-16.punch: HACOR (heart rate, acidosis, consciousness, oxygenation, rate) above 5 after 1 hour of NIV predicts failure in over 80%, so intubate early; for NIV a higher score is worse.

ARDS-17.sub: Respiratory → ARDS → Patient self-inflicted lung injury
ARDS-17.intro: Why does NIV do badly in hypoxaemic failure, and why does delay matter? Because the patient’s own breathing can injure the lung. A high respiratory drive generates large swings in pleural pressure, and the lung feels transpulmonary pressure, not the modest airway pressure on the screen.
why: **Lung injury caused by the patient’s own vigorous spontaneous effort, on NIV, HFNC or assisted modes.** Hypoxaemia, acidosis and inflammation drive breathing hard; in an injured, small lung, those big breaths over-stretch it in the same way that a large ventilator breath would (ARDS-18).

**Large negative pleural swings → high transpulmonary pressure and tidal volume; pendelluft (gas moving from non-dependent to dependent lung); raised transmural vascular pressure → oedema; patient–ventilator dyssynchrony.** On NIV, the ventilator’s pressure support and the patient’s muscle pressure add together, so large tidal volumes are easy to reach: in Carteaux’s cohort, patients who failed NIV averaged about 10.6 mL/kg PBW, against 8.5 in those who succeeded. In an injured lung, a forceful diaphragm contraction sucks gas from non-dependent into dependent alveoli before air enters from the mouth (pendelluft), stretching the dependent lung in a way the airway pressure does not show. Very negative pleural pressure also lowers the pressure around the capillaries, raising the transmural pressure across them and adding oedema. Dyssynchrony, such as double triggering, stacks breaths.

**Do not delay intubation in a patient with high drive; then sedation, higher PEEP, or neuromuscular blockade.** On NIV for hypoxaemic failure, an expired tidal volume persistently above about 9.5 mL/kg PBW (Carteaux 2016) predicts NIV failure, mainly when P/F is ≤200, even in a patient who looks comfortable — and NIV failure with late intubation carries a high mortality. After intubation, sedation lowers the drive, higher PEEP makes the injured lung behave more uniformly and reduces pendelluft, and paralysis abolishes the effort entirely in severe cases.
mimic: P-SILI vs VILI
Same physics, different source of pressure: the patient’s muscles in P-SILI, the ventilator in VILI.
traps: “She is comfortable, so tidal volumes of >9.5 mL/kg on NIV do not matter”
Read the volume, not the face: it marks high drive and P-SILI risk, and predicts NIV failure (81–94% got this right).
“High tidal volume on NPPV causes auto-PEEP or prevents recruitment”
The concern is P-SILI. The keyed wording ‘a marker of low lung compliance’ is loose: a large tidal volume marks high drive, which is dangerous because the lung receiving it is small.
“Airway pressure on NIV is low, so the lung is safe”
Transpulmonary pressure can be dangerously high while airway pressure looks safe.
decode: Hypoxaemic failure on NIV, comfortable, tidal volumes consistently >9.5 mL/kg — main concern? [DocT GT, two tests]
Patient self-inflicted lung injury.
NPPV in de novo hypoxaemic failure — concern about high tidal volumes? [DocT GT]
P-SILI.
Causes of NIV failure in ARDS [NEET 2024]
P-SILI, delayed intubation, mask intolerance, secretions, shock.
ARDS-17.punch: A patient with high drive can injure his own lung through large pleural swings and pendelluft, unseen on the airway pressure; a tidal volume above about 9.5 mL/kg on NIV is the warning, and early intubation is the remedy.

ARDS-18.intro: The ventilator can do to the lung what the patient’s effort does in P-SILI. Each type of VILI names a different way the breath harms the lung, and each is matched by a setting that prevents it — which is how the questions are framed.
why: **Volutrauma: over-distension from high tidal volume (high strain).** Animal work (Dreyfuss) showed that it is the volume, not the airway pressure itself, that injures: high pressure with the chest strapped, limiting volume, caused little oedema, whereas high volume at low pressure caused severe injury. Low tidal volume prevents it.

**Barotrauma: high transpulmonary pressure → air leak (pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum).** Over-stretched alveoli rupture, and air tracks along the bronchovascular sheaths into the mediastinum and under the skin, where on a chest X-ray it can outline the fibres of pectoralis major (the ‘ginkgo leaf’ sign).

**Atelectrauma: cyclic opening and closing of unstable units; shear (low PEEP).** Units that collapse at end-expiration and are forced open with each breath tear at the junction between open and closed lung. Enough PEEP keeps them open, which is why PEEP is started early, not just to raise the PaO₂.

**Biotrauma: mediator release from injured lung → distant organ failure.** Injurious ventilation releases cytokines into the blood; lower tidal volumes reduce them, which is one explanation of why ARMA lowered organ failure as well as mortality (ARDS-19).
**Ergotrauma: injury from total energy delivered (mechanical power) (standard teaching, not in your notes).** It brings rate and flow into the picture, not only volume and pressure (ARDS-27).

**Strain = tidal volume ÷ end-expiratory lung volume; stress = transpulmonary pressure.** Strain is how much the open lung is stretched relative to its resting size; stress is the pressure across it. They are linked by the specific elastance of the lung (stress = specific elastance × strain), so the same tidal volume is more harmful in a smaller baby lung.
mimic: Volutrauma vs barotrauma
Volutrauma is diffuse oedema from over-stretch; barotrauma is air outside the alveoli.
traps: “High PEEP is mainly to improve cardiac output or prevent hypercapnia”
PEEP raises intrathoracic pressure and can lower cardiac output; its purposes are recruitment, a larger end-expiratory lung volume (FRC) and prevention of atelectrauma (98% got this right).
“Barotrauma is caused by high airway pressure per se”
The injury follows high transpulmonary pressure and volume; airway pressure is only a proxy.
decode: FiO₂ 0.7, plateau 32 — strongest reason to start PEEP early? [DocT GT]
Prevent ventilator-induced lung injury (atelectrauma).
Primary rationale for high PEEP in ARDS [DocT QBank]
Recruits collapsed alveoli and increases FRC.
Post-ROSC, difficult bag-mask ventilation — expected chest X-ray finding? [Marrow]
Ginkgo leaf sign: subcutaneous emphysema outlining pectoralis major, from air leak.
ARDS-18.punch: Volume over-stretches, cyclic collapse shears, the injured lung releases mediators and the total energy adds up; low tidal volume and enough PEEP are the two settings that prevent most of it.

ARDS-19.intro: ARMA is the trial that turned the baby-lung idea (ARDS-10) into practice. It is the only ventilator setting in ARDS with a large mortality benefit in a randomised trial, so it is the answer to most ‘which strategy improves survival’ questions.
why: **Tidal volume 6 vs 12 mL/kg predicted body weight (861 patients).** The ARDS Network trial (NEJM 2000) compared a low tidal volume with what was then standard practice.
**Plateau ≤30 vs ≤50 cmH₂O.** The tidal volume in the low arm was reduced further, down to 4 mL/kg, if the plateau stayed above 30 (ARDS-22).
**31.0% vs 39.8% mortality (about 9% absolute reduction); stopped early for benefit.** About one death prevented for every 11 patients treated.

**More ventilator-free and organ-failure-free days.** Oxygenation was initially worse in the low-volume arm, yet survival was better: the benefit came from less lung injury, not from better gas exchange — so a better PaO₂ is not the goal of ventilation.
mimic: Therapies that improve oxygenation vs therapies that improve survival
Inhaled vasodilators and recruitment manoeuvres raise PaO₂ without proven survival benefit; low tidal volume (and proning in severe ARDS) improves survival.
traps: “Plateau pressure <35 cmH₂O” as the goal
The ARDSNet limit is ≤30.
“Intubated with P/F 86 on FiO₂ 1.0 — start VV-ECMO” (only 66% chose low tidal volume)
First ventilate protectively: 4–6 mL/kg with PEEP >5, then prone. ECMO comes after optimised ventilation fails (EOLIA criteria: P/F <50 for >3 h, <80 for >6 h, or pH <7.25 with PaCO₂ ≥60 for >6 h).
“Use actual body weight”
Predicted body weight, from height and sex (ARDS-21). Stems that say ‘ideal body weight’ mean the same thing.
decode: Primary goal of lung-protective ventilation in ARDS [DocT QBank]
Tidal volume 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight (79% got this right).
Strategy most likely to reduce ventilator-associated lung injury [DocT QBank]
Low tidal volume (6 mL/kg ideal body weight) with appropriate PEEP.
Influenza, intubated, P/F 86 on FiO₂ 1.0 — next best step? [DocT GT]
Tidal volume 4–6 mL/kg with PEEP >5, not ECMO or CT.
ARDS-19.punch: ARMA: 6 mL/kg predicted body weight with plateau ≤30 cut mortality from 39.8% to 31.0% despite worse early oxygenation — protecting the lung, not the PaO₂, is what saves lives.

ARDS-20.sub: Respiratory → ARDS → Higher vs lower PEEP
ARDS-20.intro: After tidal volume, the next question was how much PEEP. Three trials compared higher and lower PEEP on top of low tidal volume, and the answer lies in who was studied.
why: **ALVEOLI, LOVS, ExPress.** ALVEOLI (ARDSNet, 2004) used a higher PEEP/FiO₂ table; LOVS (2008) added recruitment manoeuvres and pressure control; ExPress (2008) raised PEEP as far as a plateau of 28–30 cmH₂O allowed.

**No mortality difference; better oxygenation and less rescue therapy with higher PEEP.** Higher PEEP recruits lung and lowers FiO₂ needs, but in patients with little recruitable lung it only over-distends what is already open, so the net effect on survival was neutral.

**Moderate to severe ARDS (P/F ≤200) benefits from higher PEEP; mild ARDS may be harmed.** The individual-patient meta-analysis of the three trials (Briel, JAMA 2010) found lower mortality with higher PEEP when P/F was ≤200, and a non-significant trend to harm above 200. ATS guidance (2024 update) suggests higher PEEP, without prolonged recruitment manoeuvres, in moderate–severe ARDS; a later trial of recruitment plus PEEP titration (ART, 2017) increased mortality.
mimic: Higher PEEP vs recruitment manoeuvres
Higher PEEP is suggested in moderate–severe ARDS; prolonged high-pressure recruitment manoeuvres are not.
traps: “Higher PEEP reduced mortality in ALVEOLI”
No trial showed it alone; the benefit appears only in pooled data for P/F ≤200 (ARDS-29e).
decode: Septic shock, bilateral infiltrates, P/F 100 — ideal ventilator settings? [Marrow]
Low tidal volume with high PEEP.
[pattern] Which ARDS patients benefit from higher PEEP?
Moderate to severe (P/F ≤200).
ARDS-20.punch: ALVEOLI, LOVS and ExPress each found no mortality difference with higher PEEP, but pooled data favour it when P/F is ≤200.

ARDS-21.intro: Every tidal volume in the ARDSNet protocol is per kilogram of predicted body weight, so this calculation comes before the first setting.
why: **Men: 50 + 0.91 × (height in cm – 152.4).** A 170 cm man: 50 + 0.91 × 17.6 = 66 kg, so 6 mL/kg is about 400 mL.
**Women: 45.5 + 0.91 × (height in cm – 152.4).** At the same height a woman’s PBW is 4.5 kg less: a 160 cm woman is about 52 kg, so 6 mL/kg is about 315 mL.
**Lung size follows height and sex, not actual weight.** Fat does not add alveoli, so dosing by actual weight gives an obese patient a dangerously large breath.
mimic: Predicted vs ideal body weight
Questions use the terms interchangeably; both mean the height-and-sex formula.
traps: “Tidal volume by actual body weight”
Never: by predicted body weight (ARDS-29a).
decode: [pattern] 170 cm man weighing 110 kg — tidal volume at 6 mL/kg?
About 400 mL, from PBW 66 kg, not 660 mL.
ARDS-21.punch: Predicted body weight is 50 (men) or 45.5 (women) + 0.91 × (height in cm – 152.4), because lung size follows height and sex, not weight.

ARDS-22.intro: This is ARMA turned into steps at the bedside. The questions test three things: the tidal volume and plateau rules, what to do when the CO₂ rises, and when hypercapnia is itself dangerous.
why: **Start 8 mL/kg PBW; reduce by 1 mL/kg every ≤2 h to 6 mL/kg.** The mode is volume assist-control. Stepping down lets the CO₂ and pH adjust gradually instead of in one jump.
**Rate up to 35/min.** The initial rate is set to match the patient’s previous minute ventilation; raising the rate is the first lever for the CO₂ that rises when tidal volume falls.

**Plateau ≤30 cmH₂O; if higher, reduce tidal volume in 1 mL/kg steps to a minimum of 4 mL/kg.** Plateau is checked with a 0.5 s inspiratory pause. Six mL/kg is a starting point: if the plateau is still high, the baby lung is smaller than average and the breath must shrink further.

**pH 7.30–7.45. If pH falls, raise rate to 35; if pH <7.15 at rate 35, tidal volume may be raised and bicarbonate considered (permissive hypercapnia).** The CO₂ is allowed to rise because protecting the lung matters more than a normal PaCO₂, and it should rise gradually, so that cells buffer it and the pH falls less. Hypercapnia is not harmless: it raises intracranial pressure by dilating cerebral vessels, constricts pulmonary vessels (raising right-ventricular afterload), depresses myocardial contractility, stimulates a sympathetic surge and shifts the oxyhaemoglobin curve to the right. So it is avoided in raised ICP and used with care in right-ventricular failure.
mimic: Permissive hypercapnia vs chasing a normal PaCO₂
Raising tidal volume to normalise CO₂ undoes the lung protection; ARDSNet raises the rate first and the volume only below pH 7.15.
traps: “PaCO₂ 76 in the first hour — raise it faster, or accept SaO₂ 75%”
Let it rise gradually on the current settings; the oxygen target stays at SpO₂ 88–95% (ARDS-23) (100% got this right).
“Hypercapnia lowers ICP”
It raises ICP through cerebral vasodilation — the ‘NOT deleterious’ answer is decreased ICP.
“pH 7.27 on 6 mL/kg — continue current settings” (Marrow key)

Permissive hypercapnia is right in principle, and the tidal volume should not be raised. But by ARDSNet, pH 7.15–7.30 means raise the rate towards 35 if it is lower; choose ‘continue’ only if the options are between that and raising tidal volume. Conversely, Marrow keys ‘increase rate’ at pH 7.32 — the lever is right, but 7.32 is already within the goal.
“Your notes: pH goal above 7.2”
Many texts accept ≥7.20 in permissive hypercapnia; the ARDSNet protocol goal is 7.30–7.45.
decode: Pneumonia ARDS, P/F 120, AKI, MODS — ARDSNet strategy? [DocT QBank]
Low tidal volume (4–8 mL/kg PBW) with plateau <30 cmH₂O.
Influenza ARDS, normal echo, VT 500 — which therapy is best shown to improve survival? [DocT GT]

6 mL/kg ideal body weight — not diuresis, inhaled vasodilators or recruitment-guided PEEP titration (none has a proven survival benefit, and recruitment with PEEP titration increased mortality in ART).
Permissive hypercapnia, PaCO₂ 76 in the first hour — next step? [DocT GT]
Maintain settings and let it rise gradually.
On 6 mL/kg: pH 7.32/PaCO₂ 48, or pH 7.27/PaCO₂ 60 — next ventilator step? [Marrow]
The lever is the respiratory rate (to 35), not the tidal volume; Marrow keys ‘increase rate’ at 7.32 and ‘continue’ at 7.27.
ARDS-22.punch: Start at 8 mL/kg PBW, step to 6 (down to 4 if plateau >30), raise the rate to 35 for acidosis, and raise tidal volume only when pH is <7.15 at rate 35 — hypercapnia is tolerated, except where ICP is raised.

parts.q: Harmful effects of hypercapnia?
parts.a: **Raised ICP** (cerebral vasodilation), **pulmonary vasoconstriction** with right-ventricular strain, **reduced myocardial contractility**, sympathetic surge and arrhythmias, **right shift of the oxyhaemoglobin curve**. Decreased ICP is not one of them.

ARDS-23.intro: The last part of the protocol sets how much oxygen is enough, and how FiO₂ and PEEP climb together to reach it.
why: **PaO₂ 55–80 mmHg; SpO₂ 88–95%.** Above this range extra oxygen adds little to delivery, while the FiO₂ and PEEP needed to reach it add their own harm. Going lower is not free either: a trial of a more conservative target in ARDS (LOCO2, PaO₂ 55–70) was stopped early with a signal of harm: higher 90-day mortality and cases of mesenteric ischaemia in the conservative arm.

**Lower PEEP/FiO₂ table: 0.3/5, 0.4/5–8, 0.5/8–10, 0.6/10, 0.7/10–14, 0.8/14, 0.9/14–18, 1.0/18–24.** If the target is not met, move to the next pair; if it is exceeded, step back. PEEP of 10 belongs with FiO₂ of about 0.5–0.7. This is the table ARMA used; the higher table, from ALVEOLI, pairs each FiO₂ with more PEEP (ARDS-20).
traps: “Aim for SpO₂ 100% or PaO₂ >100”
The target is deliberately modest; hyperoxia is not the aim.
decode: Which settings are most consistent with lung-protective ventilation? [DocT QBank]
Tidal volume 6 mL/kg with PEEP 10 (86% got this right).
[pattern] ARDSNet SpO₂ target
ARDS-23.punch: ARDSNet aims for PaO₂ 55–80 and SpO₂ 88–95%, climbing the PEEP/FiO₂ table in pairs until the target is reached.

ARDS-24.intro: The plateau rule in ARDS-22 depends on reading the airway pressure curve. In volume control with constant flow, a pause at end-inspiration splits the peak into its two parts.
why: **Resistive pressure (airways, tube): flow × resistance.** When flow stops, this part disappears, so the pressure falls from peak to plateau.
**Driving pressure: the elastic load of the tidal volume.** It is the pressure needed to hold the breath in the lung against its elastic recoil (ARDS-26).

**End-inspiratory hold of 0.5–2 s (zero flow), in a passive patient.** With no flow, airway pressure equals alveolar pressure; an active patient’s effort distorts the reading. Total PEEP needs a separate end-expiratory hold, to include any auto-PEEP.
traps: “Peak pressure reflects lung stretch”
Peak includes the resistive pressure; plateau reflects the stretch.
decode: [pattern] Peak pressure rises from 30 to 45, plateau unchanged at 22 — cause?
A resistance problem: bronchospasm, secretions or a kinked tube.
ARDS-24.punch: Peak minus plateau is resistance, plateau minus PEEP is the elastic load; the plateau needs a no-flow hold in a passive patient.

Meaning
Causes
