ARDS-25.intro: Each named pressure on a ventilator is a difference between two points along the path from the ventilator to the pleura. Knowing which two points each spans answers both the calculation questions and the subtler question of when the airway pressure can be trusted.
why: **Pplat – PEEP = driving pressure, which reflects tidal volume ÷ compliance.** Use the total PEEP (set plus auto-PEEP).

**Ppeak – Pplat = resistive pressure, which reflects airway resistance.** This only works in volume control with constant flow; in pressure control the peak is the set pressure, and flow decays, so this gap does not measure resistance.
**Palv – Ppl = transpulmonary pressure: stress on the lung itself.** This is what over-stretches alveoli (ARDS-28).
**Palv – Patm = trans-respiratory pressure: lung plus chest wall.** In a passive patient at zero flow, this is the plateau; it treats the lung and chest wall as one.
**Ppl – Patm = chest-wall pressure: the chest wall alone.** A stiff chest wall (obesity, abdominal hypertension) takes a larger share of the plateau, so the plateau overstates lung stress.
mimic: Respiratory-system vs lung compliance
Volume ÷ (plateau – PEEP) gives respiratory-system compliance; lung compliance needs pleural (oesophageal) pressure.
traps: “Alveolar pressure during the hold is 32 (peak), 18 (plateau – PEEP) or 26” (62–81% chose 24)
At zero flow, airway pressure equals alveolar pressure: the plateau, 24. 18 is the driving pressure; 32 still includes the resistive part.
“Pressure control, paralysed asthmatic: compliance is reliable from Pinsp and volume, or resistance from peak – pause” (only 12% got this right)

Both statements hold only in other circumstances. In pressure control, peak is the set pressure, so peak – pause cannot give resistance; and with flow not reaching zero, or auto-PEEP in an asthmatic, Pinsp – PEEP is not the true elastic pressure. The keyed answer: once paralysis wears off, the patient’s own muscle pressure adds to the ventilator’s, so pleural (oesophageal) pressure is needed to calculate lung compliance.
decode: Volume control, end-inspiratory hold: peak 32, plateau 24, PEEP 6 — alveolar pressure? [DocT QBank, DocT GT, three tests]
24 cmH₂O (the plateau).
Asthmatic on pressure control, paralysed, VT 200 mL on Pinsp 25/PEEP 5 — most accurate statement? [DocT GT]
When paralysis wears off, pleural pressure is needed to calculate pulmonary compliance reliably.
ARDS-25.punch: Plateau is alveolar pressure; plateau minus PEEP is driving pressure, peak minus plateau is resistance (in volume control only), and only pleural pressure separates the lung from the chest wall.

ARDS-26.intro: Driving pressure brings the deck back to the baby lung. Six mL/kg PBW assumes an average lung; driving pressure measures the breath against the lung that is actually open.
why: **Pplat – PEEP = tidal volume ÷ respiratory-system compliance.** 400 mL into a compliance of 25 mL/cmH₂O needs 16 cmH₂O.

**Amato, 2015: of all ventilator variables it was the one most strongly linked to survival; changes in tidal volume or PEEP helped only if they lowered it.** A re-analysis of 3562 patients from nine trials: each rise of one standard deviation (about 7 cmH₂O) carried about 1.4 times the risk of death (relative risk 1.41). This is an association from secondary analysis, not a randomised test of a driving-pressure target.

**It scales tidal volume to the size of the baby lung (compliance) rather than to predicted body weight.** Two patients with the same height get the same 6 mL/kg, but in the one with less open lung that breath is a larger strain; driving pressure shows it. PEEP that recruits lung raises compliance and lowers driving pressure; PEEP that only over-distends raises it.
mimic: Driving pressure vs peak pressure
Driving pressure uses plateau, not peak, and total PEEP.
traps: “High PEEP or a high peak pressure predicts a better outcome”
Low driving pressure does.
decode: Predictor of a better outcome in ARDS [DocT GT PYQ; NEET 2024]
Low driving pressure (<14–15).
ARDS-26.punch: Driving pressure (plateau – PEEP = VT/compliance) sizes the breath to the open lung; below 15 is the target, and in Amato’s analysis it was the ventilator variable most strongly associated with survival.

ARDS-27.intro: Driving pressure looks at one breath. Mechanical power asks how much energy the lung receives every minute, which also counts how often the breath is given and how fast it is pushed in.
why: **Energy delivered to the respiratory system per minute (J/min).** Energy per breath (pressure × volume) multiplied by the respiratory rate.

**0.098 × RR × VT × (Ppeak – ½ driving pressure), VT in litres; bedside surrogate (4 × driving pressure) + RR.** The 0.098 converts L·cmH₂O to joules. RR 20, VT 0.4 L, peak 30, driving pressure 14: 0.098 × 20 × 0.4 × 23 ≈ 18 J/min.
**Tidal volume, driving pressure, flow, PEEP and respiratory rate.** Flow enters through the resistive part of the peak pressure, PEEP through the static part.

**Above about 17 J/min (12 J/min in ARDS in some studies) (standard teaching, not in your notes).** The 17 J/min figure is an association with mortality in large observational ICU data (Serpa Neto 2018); the 12 J/min figure comes mainly from experimental work. No randomised trial has tested a power target.
mimic: Mechanical power vs driving pressure
Driving pressure ignores rate; power counts it, so a very high rate used to compensate for a low tidal volume is not harmless.
traps: “Mechanical power is airway pressure × time, or pressure × compliance, or excludes PEEP” (only 34% got this right)
Energy is pressure × volume, not pressure × time; pressure × compliance gives a volume. Power is energy per breath × rate, and PEEP is one of its components.
decode: Best description of mechanical power [DocT GT]
The product of energy per breath and respiratory rate.
ARDS-27.punch: Mechanical power is energy per breath times rate (J/min), counting volume, pressure, flow, PEEP and rate; values above about 17 J/min are associated with higher mortality.

ARDS-28.intro: The plateau tells you the pressure across lung and chest wall together (ARDS-25). When the chest wall is stiff, part of that pressure never reaches the lung, and an oesophageal balloon is the way to separate the two.
why: **Alveolar pressure (airway pressure at zero flow) – pleural pressure; pleural pressure from an oesophageal balloon in the lower third of the oesophagus.** The oesophagus lies against the pleura, so its pressure approximates pleural pressure; position is checked by an occlusion test, in which airway and oesophageal pressure swings should match.

**Positive, about 0 to +3 cmH₂O (EPVent protocol used 0–10), so alveoli stay open; this is how PEEP is titrated.** A negative end-expiratory value means pleural pressure exceeds airway pressure, so dependent alveoli are squeezed shut; PEEP is raised until it is just positive.

**Stiff chest wall: obesity, raised intra-abdominal pressure, chest-wall oedema; plateau pressure overestimates lung stress here.** A morbidly obese patient may tolerate, and need, a PEEP and plateau that would be excessive in a thin one.
mimic: Oesophageal pressure vs alveolar pressure
Pes approximates pleural pressure, not alveolar, and it is affected by the weight of the chest wall and mediastinum.
traps: “PL = Paw + Pes” or “keep end-inspiratory PL above 35”
PL = Paw – Pes; end-inspiratory PL is kept below about 25.
“Oesophageal-guided PEEP is proven better”
EPVent-2 found it no better than an empirical high-PEEP table (standard teaching, not in your notes).
decode: Obese ARDS, end-expiratory Pes 20, PEEP 15 — interpretation? [DocT GT]
PL –5 cmH₂O: dependent alveoli likely collapsed; PEEP should be raised.
ARDS-28.punch: Transpulmonary pressure is airway minus oesophageal pressure; keep it just positive at end-expiration and below about 25 at end-inspiration — most useful when a stiff chest wall makes the plateau misleading.

ARDS-29.sub: Respiratory → ARDS → Revision: true or false
ARDS-29.intro: A sweep through the deck. Each statement turns on one detail from an earlier card.
why: **False — ARMA used predicted body weight** (ARDS-19, ARDS-21).
**False — a ROX of 5 at 12 h is ≥4.88, which predicts HFNC success** (ARDS-15).
**True — HACOR above 5 at 1 h predicts NIV failure in over 80%** (ARDS-16).
**False — driving pressure is plateau – PEEP, not peak – PEEP** (ARDS-26).
**False — ALVEOLI showed no mortality difference with higher PEEP** (ARDS-20).
**True — the ARDSNet SpO₂ target is 88–95%, with PaO₂ 55–80** (ARDS-23).
**True — PEEP prevents atelectrauma by stopping cyclic collapse** (ARDS-18).
traps: “A higher ROX is worse”
Lower ROX is worse; higher HACOR is worse.
decode: ROX formula on HFNC [DocT GT]
SpO₂/FiO₂ ÷ RR (83% got this right).
[pattern] Statements about scores and trials
ROX lower is worse, HACOR higher is worse; ARMA used PBW; no single PEEP trial cut mortality.
ARDS-29.punch: Most errors here come from direction (low ROX, high HACOR are bad), the plateau-not-peak rule and the negative PEEP trials.

spine: Supporting the patient before intubation
High-flow nasal oxygen is the first-line non-invasive support in hypoxaemic failure, NIV is kept for mild cases, and ROX and HACOR tell you early when each is failing.
How breathing and ventilators injure

The lung is injured by the stretch it actually feels — from the patient’s own vigorous effort (P-SILI) or from the ventilator (volutrauma, atelectrauma, biotrauma) — so stress and strain, not airway pressure alone, are what matter.
Trials behind lung-protective ventilation
ARMA showed that 6 mL/kg predicted body weight saves lives; higher PEEP did not change mortality in three trials, but may help when P/F is ≤200.
Setting the ARDSNet ventilator

Calculate predicted body weight from height and sex, step tidal volume down to 6 mL/kg, keep plateau ≤30, accept hypercapnia within the pH rules, and pair FiO₂ with PEEP from the table to a modest oxygen target.
Reading the pressures on screen
A hold at end-inspiration separates peak (resistance plus elastance) from plateau (alveolar pressure), and an oesophageal balloon separates the lung from the chest wall.
Driving pressure, power and review
Driving pressure scales the breath to the open lung and is the variable most strongly associated with survival; mechanical power adds rate and flow to measure the total energy the lung receives.
RESP01B.primer: Respiratory-system compliance is tidal volume divided by the pressure needed to hold it (plateau minus PEEP); in ARDS it is low because the aerated ‘baby lung’ is small, not because that lung is stiff (ARDS-10). Plateau pressure is the airway pressure during a short pause at the end of inspiration with no flow, so it equals alveolar pressure; peak pressure also includes the pressure spent pushing flow through the tube and airways. What actually stretches the lung is transpulmonary pressure — alveolar minus pleural pressure — so a strongly breathing patient can over-stretch his lung even when the airway pressure looks low. HFNC delivers heated, humidified gas at up to 60 L/min through nasal prongs; NIV delivers set pressures (inspiratory support plus PEEP, or CPAP) through a sealed mask.

ARDS-30.intro: Once lung-protective ventilation is running and the P/F ratio is still below 150, the next step with a proven survival benefit is prone positioning. PROSEVA is the trial behind every number examiners ask: the P/F threshold, the hours per day and the size of the benefit.
why: **P/F <150 on FiO₂ ≥0.6, PEEP ≥5 and tidal volume about 6 mL/kg, confirmed after 12–24 h of stabilisation.** The stabilisation period matters: many patients improve once ventilation is optimised, so only those still below 150 after 12–24 h were enrolled — moderate-to-severe ARDS, not mild. That is why <150 is the keyed threshold, not <200 or <100.

**Within 36 h of intubation; sessions of at least 16 h a day (your notes: 12–18 h).** PROSEVA proned early and for long sessions (average about 17 h); patients stayed prone daily until oxygenation held in the supine position. Short sessions let the dorsal lung collapse again each time the patient is turned back.

**28-day mortality 16.0% vs 32.8%.** A halving of mortality, and the benefit persisted at 90 days. Current guidance recommends prolonged prone sessions — ESICM 2023 more than 16 h a day in moderate-to-severe ARDS, ATS more than 12 h a day in severe ARDS; it comes before ECMO, not after it (ARDS-35).
mimic: PROSEVA vs the earlier prone trials
Earlier trials proned later, for shorter sessions (some about 7 h a day) and included milder ARDS; they improved oxygenation but not survival. PROSEVA changed all three.
Prone vs ECMO for refractory hypoxaemia
Prone has a proven mortality benefit and is tried first; ECMO is for hypoxaemia that persists despite prone (ARDS-35).
traps: “Prone for at least 6 h a day is enough”
PROSEVA used ≥16 h; 6 h is a distractor. One DocT GT paper prints the keyed option as ‘≤16 hours/day’ — a misprint; pick the prone option whatever sign is printed.
“P/F 105 on FiO₂ 1.0, PEEP 8, paralysed — start ECMO, inhaled NO or oesophageal-pressure PEEP” (only 59% chose prone)

P/F 105 is below 150 and prone has not been tried, so prone is next. ECMO is not yet indicated (P/F not <80 and prone not tried), inhaled NO improves only oxygenation, and oesophageal-pressure-guided PEEP had no outcome benefit (EPVent-2).
“Avoid prone in severe ARDS”
The reverse: prone is recommended in moderate-to-severe ARDS, and severe ARDS is where it matters most. This was the NEET 2025 ‘should NOT be done’ answer.
“Proning improves oxygenation but does not affect mortality”
PROSEVA halved 28-day mortality.
“Methylprednisolone 2 mg/kg/day gives the most mortality benefit” (DocT GT distractor)

Prone ≥16 h has the largest and most consistent mortality benefit, so it is the answer. Early corticosteroids are now conditionally recommended (DEXA-ARDS; ATS 2024, SCCM 2024; ARDS-40), but that is weaker evidence than PROSEVA, and 2 mg/kg/day is not the regimen behind the current recommendation.
decode: At what P/F ratio is prone positioning recommended? [NEET 2024, DocT GT]
Moderate ARDS, P/F 140 on PEEP 10 — which intervention gives the most mortality benefit? [DocT GT]
Prone ≥16 h a day.
Intubated pneumonia, P/F 105 on FiO₂ 1.0, PEEP 8, paralysed — next step? [DocT GT]
Prone the patient.
Moderate–severe ARDS: which should NOT be done about prone ventilation? [NEET 2025]
Avoiding prone in severe ARDS.
ARDS-30.punch: PROSEVA: P/F <150 on FiO₂ ≥0.6 after 12–24 h, proned within 36 h for ≥16 h a day, cut 28-day mortality from 32.8% to 16.0% — so prone comes before ECMO, nitric oxide or HFOV.

ARDS-31.intro: Why should turning a patient over halve mortality? In the supine ARDS lung, the weight of the oedematous lung, the heart and the abdomen squeeze the dorsal regions shut, so a small ventral lung takes every breath. Turning the patient prone changes where that weight falls.
why: **The pleural-pressure gradient becomes more uniform and the dorsal lung is recruited (more lung mass lies dorsally).** Supine, pleural pressure is much less negative over the dependent dorsal lung, so it collapses. Prone, the dorsal lung becomes non-dependent and re-opens, and because more of the lung’s tissue lies dorsally, more lung is gained there than is lost ventrally. The shape of the lung also fits the chest wall better prone, so ventilation spreads more evenly.

**Perfusion stays mainly dorsal, so V/Q matching improves and shunt falls.** Pulmonary blood flow goes mostly to the dorsal lung whichever way the patient lies. Supine, that well-perfused lung was the collapsed part — shunt; prone, it is re-aerated, so ventilation and perfusion now meet in the same regions.

**The heart and abdomen no longer compress the lung; the right ventricle is unloaded; secretions drain.** Prone, the heart rests on the sternum rather than on the lower lobes. Recruitment and a lower PaCO₂ reduce pulmonary vascular resistance, which offloads a strained right ventricle (acute cor pulmonale, ARDS-43). Gravity drains secretions from the dorsal airways.

**More homogeneous strain → less VILI.** When ventilation is spread over more open lung, each alveolus is stretched less, and fewer units open and close with every breath. This, not the higher PaO₂, is thought to be why survival improves.
mimic: Oxygenation response vs survival benefit
In PROSEVA, the gain in PaO₂ after proning did not predict who survived; patients whose PaO₂ does not rise still benefit, so a non-responder is not a reason to stop.
Prone vs raising mean airway pressure
Inverse-ratio ventilation, HFOV and recruitment manoeuvres open lung with pressure; prone opens it by redistributing weight, without raising pressure.
traps: “Proning works by raising mean airway pressure”, “by reducing dead space through airway patency” or “by improving chest-wall compliance”

Its main effect is redistribution of ventilation to the dorsal lung, where perfusion already is. The keyed options say ‘V/Q matching by redistributing ventilation to dorsal regions’ or ‘to more compliant regions’.
“The main goal of proning is to prevent pressure sores or remove lung fluid”
Pressure sores are a complication of proning (ARDS-32); the goal is recruitment and oxygenation.
“Severe ARDS, FiO₂ 0.8, Pplat 30, pH 7.22 — increase VT, reduce PEEP or target PaCO₂ <40” (DocT keys inverse-ratio ventilation)

With prone not offered, IRV is the least harmful option because it raises mean airway pressure without raising tidal volume or plateau pressure. It has no outcome evidence and is in no ARDS guideline; pH 7.22 is acceptable permissive hypercapnia, so do not chase PaCO₂ <40. If prone is offered, choose prone.
decode: Primary mechanism by which proning improves oxygenation? [DocT]
Better V/Q matching by redistributing ventilation to the dorsal lung.
Image of a prone patient — primary goal of this position? [DocT]
Alveolar recruitment and oxygenation.
Which statement about proning is true? (≥6 h, ‘no mortality effect’ as distractors) [DocT]
It improves oxygenation by redistributing ventilation and perfusion.
Severe ARDS, Pplat 30, pH 7.22, no prone option — best strategy to improve oxygenation without VILI? [DocT, DocT GT]
Inverse-ratio ventilation (best of the options; prone if offered).
ARDS-31.punch: Prone re-opens the heavy dorsal lung where the blood already flows, so V/Q improves; its survival benefit comes from spreading strain evenly and reducing VILI, not from the rise in PaO₂.

ARDS-32.sub: Respiratory → ARDS → Prone positioning: contraindications and complications
ARDS-32.intro: Prone is the step that saves lives, so the questions test when you cannot do it — and then what comes instead — and what goes wrong when you do.
why: **Contraindications: unstable spine (absolute); raised intracranial pressure; open chest or abdomen; recent sternotomy or tracheal surgery; facial or pelvic fractures; massive haemoptysis; severe haemodynamic instability; life-threatening arrhythmia; late pregnancy (relative).** Each is either something turning could injure (an unstable spine, fresh wounds, fractures that bear weight face-down), something prone worsens (prone with the head turned can raise ICP and impede venous drainage), or a patient who cannot be resuscitated face-down. When prone is contraindicated and the patient meets EOLIA criteria, VV-ECMO is the next step (ARDS-35).

**Complications: tube obstruction or displacement; loss of lines and drains; pressure sores (face, chest, knees); facial and eye oedema; brachial plexus injury; feed intolerance and vomiting; transient desaturation.** The dangerous ones happen during the turn — the tube and lines. Pressure sores are the commonest, on the face, chest and knees, which bear the weight. Facial and eye oedema, and eye injury from pressure, are why the face is padded and moved regularly.
mimic: Raised ICP as contraindication vs complication
Raised ICP is a reason not to prone; facial and ocular injury is the keyed ‘major complication’ of proning itself.
traps: “Increased intracranial pressure is the major complication of proning” (only 67% chose facial and ocular injury)
Raised ICP belongs to the contraindications. The keyed complication is facial and ocular injury, which follows from lying face-down for 16 h.
“Polytrauma with uncleared C-spine and chest lacerations, P/F <150 — prone the patient” (only 52% chose ECMO)

Prone is contraindicated (unstable spine, open chest-wall wounds). With PaO₂ 67 on FiO₂ 1.0 — P/F 67 — for 6 h despite optimal ventilation and paralysis, he meets the EOLIA oxygenation criterion (<80 for >6 h), so VV-ECMO is next.
Two correct options in one DocT GT question

‘Proning improves oxygenation by redistributing ventilation and perfusion’ is keyed, but ‘proning is contraindicated in spinal fractures’ is also true (unstable spine is absolute). Pick the keyed mechanism statement.
decode: Major complication of prone positioning? [DocT]
Facial and ocular injuries.
Uncleared C-spine, ventral chest lacerations, P/F 67 for 6 h, paralysed — next step? [DocT GT]
VV-ECMO (prone contraindicated).
Proned, ventilated TBI patient desaturates acutely — what to assess first? [Marrow]
Tube dislodgement or obstruction.
ARDS-32.punch: Do not prone an unstable spine, raised ICP, an open chest or abdomen or a peri-arrest patient; when you do prone, watch the tube and lines at every turn and the face and eyes for pressure injury.

parts.q: A proned, ventilated patient suddenly desaturates: first step?
parts.a: **Check the tube first: displacement or obstruction** (Marrow), before blaming the lung — the turn is when tubes move.

ARDS-33.intro: If collapsed lung can be re-opened with pressure, why not do it deliberately? A recruitment manoeuvre is a brief, high pressure to open collapsed alveoli, followed by enough PEEP to keep them open. The idea is sound physiology; the ART trial is why it is no longer routine.
why: **Sustained inflation: CPAP 40 cmH₂O for 30–40 s.** The pressure must exceed the opening pressure of collapsed units. The other method is stepwise (staircase) recruitment: PEEP is raised in steps, then lowered in a decremental trial while static compliance is tracked — the step at which compliance suddenly falls is the derecruitment point, and PEEP is set about 2 cmH₂O above it after re-recruiting. Whatever the method, the gain is lost unless PEEP holds the lung open afterwards.

**Hypotension (fall in venous return), barotrauma, desaturation.** High intrathoracic pressure squeezes the great veins and loads the right ventricle, so cardiac output falls during the manoeuvre. Over-stretching already-open alveoli can rupture them (pneumothorax). Oxygenation can fall transiently as blood is pushed towards unrecruited lung and output drops.

**Stepwise recruitment plus PEEP titrated to best compliance vs low PEEP: higher mortality and more barotrauma with recruitment.** ART (Cavalcanti, JAMA 2017; about 1000 patients with moderate-to-severe ARDS) found 28-day mortality 55.3% vs 49.3%, with more pneumothorax needing drainage. ESICM 2023 and the 2024 ATS update both make a strong recommendation against prolonged high-pressure recruitment manoeuvres, and ESICM also suggests (weakly) against brief high-pressure manoeuvres.
mimic: Derecruitment vs pneumothorax as a cause of sudden desaturation

After open suctioning or a disconnection, the lung derecruits and compliance falls; a pneumothorax adds unilateral absent breath sounds and haemodynamic collapse — exclude it before any recruitment manoeuvre.
traps: “Recruitment manoeuvres every 4 h maintain alveolar stability”
Routine, repeated manoeuvres are not recommended; ART showed harm.
“PEEP after a recruitment manoeuvre is to prevent over-distension or improve cardiac output”
It is there to keep open what the manoeuvre opened (DocT GT, 100% right).
“Recruitment manoeuvres are a grade B recommendation”
In the Harrison table Marrow uses, recruitment manoeuvres are grade C; low tidal volume is A, and conservative fluids, higher PEEP, prone and ECMO are B.
decode: Recommended sustained-inflation technique? [DocT GT]
CPAP 30–40 cmH₂O.
Purpose of PEEP after a recruitment manoeuvre? [DocT GT]
To maintain the recruitment achieved.
Decremental PEEP trial: static compliance suddenly falls before oxygenation worsens — what happened? [DocT GT]
Alveolar derecruitment.
Desaturation after open suctioning in ventilated pneumonia — next step? [Marrow]
Recruitment manoeuvre (after excluding pneumothorax).
ARDS-33.punch: A recruitment manoeuvre (CPAP 40 for 30–40 s) opens lung only if PEEP then holds it open, costs blood pressure and risks barotrauma — and in ART, recruitment with compliance-titrated PEEP increased mortality.

parts.q: Desaturation after open suctioning in ARDS: why, and what then?
parts.a: **Disconnection loses PEEP and the lung derecruits.** Exclude pneumothorax, then recruit; pre-oxygenate with FiO₂ 1.0 and use a closed in-line system when PEEP or FiO₂ is high (Marrow).

ARDS-34.intro: HFOV takes the open-lung idea to its limit: hold the lung open with a constant high mean airway pressure and move gas with tiny oscillations, so there is no cyclic stretch at all. In theory it is the ideal lung-protective mode; two large trials in 2013 showed it is not.
why: **OSCAR: no difference in mortality. OSCILLATE: higher mortality (stopped early).** OSCAR (UK, about 800 patients) found 30-day mortality almost identical in the two arms. OSCILLATE (Canada and elsewhere, about 550 patients) was stopped early because in-hospital mortality was higher with HFOV (about 47% vs 35%).

**High mean airway pressure → haemodynamic compromise, more vasopressors, sedation and paralysis.** HFOV holds a constant high mean airway pressure for oxygenation, which reduces venous return and raises right-ventricular afterload. In OSCILLATE, the HFOV arm needed more vasoactive drugs, midazolam and neuromuscular blockade.

**Not recommended for routine use in adult ARDS.** The ATS/ESICM/SCCM 2017 guideline makes a strong recommendation against routine HFOV in moderate-to-severe ARDS; the 2023 ESICM guideline did not revisit it.
mimic: HFOV vs high-frequency jet ventilation
HFJV pulses small jets at about 100–200/min with passive expiration; its niche is airway surgery and a large bronchopleural fistula, not ARDS. Neither improves adult ARDS survival.
OSCAR vs OSCILLATE
OSCAR: no difference. OSCILLATE: harm. NEET 2024 asked OSCAR: ‘HFO in adult ARDS — no benefit’.
traps: “HFOV provides low inspiratory pressures”
It runs a high mean airway pressure; its theoretical advantage is tiny tidal volumes at high rates, not low pressure.
“In HFOV expiration is passive” or “raising the frequency clears more CO₂”
Expiration is active; lowering the frequency lengthens each cycle, enlarges the tidal volume and clears more CO₂.
“HFOV is the preferred rescue over prone positioning”
Prone has the survival benefit; HFOV harmed or did nothing.
“The keyed ‘advantage’ means HFOV is recommended”
DocT keys the theoretical mechanism (small volumes, high rates, less VILI); the trials failed, so it is not recommended routinely.
decode: Primary advantage of HFOV in ARDS? [DocT, DocT GT]
Very small tidal volumes at very high rates, minimising VILI (in theory).
How is gas transported during HFOV? [DocT GT]
Taylor dispersion and pendelluft, with tidal volumes smaller than dead space.
Primary advantage of HFJV in ARDS? [DocT, DocT GT]
Very small tidal volumes at high rates (theory only; no outcome benefit).
OSCAR trial was about? [NEET 2024]
HFOV in adult ARDS: no benefit.
ARDS-34.punch: HFOV oxygenates with a high mean airway pressure and moves gas below the dead space, but OSCAR showed no benefit and OSCILLATE showed harm, so it is not used routinely in adult ARDS.

table.title: How HFOV works — the details the stems test
head: Feature
HFOV
rows: set by **mean airway pressure** (high, CPAP-like) and FiO₂
Taylor dispersion, pendelluft, asymmetric velocity profiles, molecular diffusion, plus bulk flow to proximal units

ARDS-35.intro: When the lung cannot exchange gas even with protective ventilation, paralysis and prone, VV-ECMO takes over that job outside the body, so the ventilator can be turned down to rest the lung. The questions test the thresholds and, above all, the order: prone first, ECMO after.
why: **P/F <80 on FiO₂ ≥0.9 despite optimal ventilation and prone (EOLIA: <50 for 3 h or <80 for 6 h).** ECMO is a rescue for persistent, severe hypoxaemia after optimal care including prone. DocT keys ‘P/F <100 despite optimal ventilation’: that is the older ELSO threshold (P/F <100 on FiO₂ >0.9 for 6 h or more despite optimal care, marking a mortality risk of 80% or more; P/F <150 marked about 50%, when ECMO should be considered), and it is still the best option when <80 is not offered.

**PaCO₂ >80 mmHg or inability to keep plateau ≤30 (EOLIA: pH <7.25 with PaCO₂ ≥60 for 6 h).** Here the problem is ventilation: the CO₂ cannot be cleared without injurious pressures. ECMO removes CO₂ very efficiently, so the ventilator can stay protective.
**Severe air-leak syndromes.** A large bronchopleural fistula leaks with every positive-pressure breath; ECMO lets the ventilator be turned right down so the leak can close.

**Ventilated >7 days at high pressures; contraindication to anticoagulation; irreversible disease; severe brain injury (standard teaching, not in your notes).** ECMO is a bridge to recovery, so it is pointless when the lung or the patient cannot recover: irreversible multi-organ failure is the keyed contraindication. Age alone is not one — it only lowers the predicted survival (RESP score).
mimic: VV vs VA ECMO
VV supports the lung only and needs a working heart; VA also supports the circulation. Severe ARDS with a normal echo → VV.
Prone vs ECMO
Prone has the proven mortality benefit and goes first; ECMO is for failure of prone or when prone is contraindicated (ARDS-32).
traps: “Refractory ARDS: ECMO” when prone positioning is also offered (DocT keys ECMO; 75% agreed)

Guidelines put prone ≥16 h a day before ECMO, and ECMO thresholds are read as ‘despite optimal ventilation’, which includes prone. If prone has not been tried, the evidence-based answer is prone; pick ECMO once prone has failed or is contraindicated.
“Persistent hypercapnia with pH <7.25” as the ECMO criterion (only 63% chose P/F <100)
Incomplete: EOLIA needs pH <7.25 with PaCO₂ ≥60 for >6 h; ‘FiO₂ >90%’ alone is also incomplete. The P/F threshold despite optimal ventilation is the cleanest answer.
“Age >60 is a contraindication”
Not in itself; irreversible multi-organ failure is.
“Recruitment manoeuvres, HFOV or a larger tidal volume” for P/F 55 after prone and paralysis
ART and OSCILLATE showed harm; with P/F 55 after optimal care, VV-ECMO is next.
Polytrauma vignette: “pH 7.25 with PaCO₂ 68 for 6 h meets EOLIA”
Strictly, EOLIA needs pH below 7.25; the stronger reason is P/F 67 on FiO₂ 1.0 for 6 h, which meets the <80 for >6 h criterion. Either way VV-ECMO is right, because prone is contraindicated.
decode: Most appropriate criterion to start ECMO in ARDS? [DocT]
P/F <100 (or <80) despite optimal ventilation, including prone.
Key contraindication to ECMO in ARDS? [DocT]
Severe, irreversible multi-organ failure.
Severe ARDS, hypoxaemic despite protective ventilation, paralysis and prone, normal echo — which configuration? [DocT GT]
Venovenous ECMO.
P/F 55 despite prone and NMB — next step? [DocT GT]
Initiate VV-ECMO.
ARDS-35.punch: VV-ECMO is for P/F <80 for 6 h, <50 for 3 h, or pH <7.25 with PaCO₂ ≥60 for 6 h despite optimal ventilation — after prone, or when prone is contraindicated — and not for irreversible disease.

table.title: EOLIA entry: any one, despite optimal ventilation
head: Criterion
Threshold

ARDS-36.intro: Two trials sit behind ECMO in ARDS, and neither alone proved it saves lives. The question is always what each actually tested and whether the result was significant.
why: **CESAR: 180 patients, transfer to an ECMO centre vs conventional care. EOLIA: 249 patients, early ECMO vs conventional ventilation with rescue ECMO.** CESAR tested a referral strategy, not ECMO itself; EOLIA tested ECMO itself, started early.

**CESAR: survival without severe disability at 6 months 63% vs 47% (RR 0.69, P = 0.03). EOLIA: 60-day mortality 35% vs 46%, P = 0.09, not significant.** EOLIA’s secondary outcome, treatment failure (death, or crossover to ECMO in the control arm), was clearly reduced — the NEET 2025 answer.

**CESAR: only 75% of the ECMO arm received ECMO; control care was not protocolised. EOLIA: 28% of controls crossed over to ECMO; stopped early.** CESAR’s benefit may reflect expert-centre care rather than ECMO. EOLIA’s crossovers diluted the difference, and it stopped for futility before reaching its planned size; later Bayesian and pooled analyses suggested a probable benefit, and the 2024 ATS update suggests VV-ECMO for selected patients with severe ARDS.
mimic: EOLIA’s two P values
0.09 for the primary outcome (60-day mortality, RR 0.76) and 0.07 for the time-to-death analysis to day 60 (hazard ratio 0.70; your notes’ ‘survival curve’); neither is significant.
traps: “EOLIA showed a significant mortality benefit”
35% vs 46%, P = 0.09: not significant (ARDS-46c).
“EOLIA showed ECMO had no effect” or “increased mortality”
The point estimate favoured ECMO and treatment failure fell; ‘no significant mortality benefit but less treatment failure’ is the keyed answer.
decode: Key findings of EOLIA? [NEET 2025]
No statistically significant mortality benefit, but reduced treatment failure.
[pattern] What did CESAR actually test?
Referral to an ECMO centre, not ECMO itself.
ARDS-36.punch: CESAR showed that referral to an ECMO centre improved survival without severe disability (63% vs 47%); EOLIA’s 35% vs 46% fell short of significance (P = 0.09) but reduced treatment failure.

ARDS-37.sub: Respiratory → ARDS → Inhaled nitric oxide and prostacyclin
ARDS-37.intro: Inhaled vasodilators are the other rescue for refractory hypoxaemia. They are a clear example of a therapy that improves the blood gas without improving survival.
why: **Selective vasodilation of ventilated units only → better V/Q matching; lowers pulmonary artery pressure without systemic hypotension.** An inhaled gas reaches only open alveoli, so only their vessels dilate and blood is drawn away from shunt units. Nitric oxide is inactivated by haemoglobin as soon as it reaches the blood, so it has no systemic effect.
**Oxygenation improves for 24–72 h; no mortality benefit.** The gain fades within a few days and no trial has shown fewer deaths; it is a bridge, for example to ECMO, not a treatment.

**Methaemoglobinaemia, nitrogen dioxide, rebound pulmonary hypertension on withdrawal, renal dysfunction.** NO oxidises haemoglobin to methaemoglobin and reacts with oxygen to form toxic NO₂, so both are monitored. Meta-analyses found more acute kidney injury with iNO. Abrupt withdrawal can cause rebound pulmonary hypertension, so it is weaned.
mimic: Inhaled vs intravenous vasodilators
Intravenous vasodilators dilate the vessels of unventilated units too, abolish hypoxic vasoconstriction and worsen shunt.
traps: “Inhaled nitric oxide improves survival”
It improves oxygenation only, and transiently (ARDS-46e).
decode: [pattern] iNO in severe ARDS — which statement is true?
Improves oxygenation transiently; no mortality benefit; renal dysfunction.
ARDS-37.punch: Inhaled vasodilators dilate only ventilated units, so V/Q improves for a day or two — but survival does not, and nitric oxide adds methaemoglobin, NO₂, rebound and kidney injury.

ARDS-38.intro: Paralysis was meant to protect the lung by stopping the patient fighting the ventilator: dyssynchrony, double-triggered breaths and big swings in transpulmonary pressure stretch the lung beyond what the settings allow. Two trials gave opposite answers, and the reason is in the control arms.
why: **Cisatracurium infusion for 48 h, early ARDS with P/F <150.** Both trials enrolled within 48 h of ARDS onset. Cisatracurium was chosen because its elimination does not depend on the liver or kidney.

**ACURASYS: better adjusted 90-day survival, less barotrauma, no excess weakness. ROSE: no difference in 90-day mortality.** ACURASYS (340 patients) found the benefit only after adjustment for baseline severity (crude 90-day mortality 31.6% vs 40.7%, P = 0.08); ROSE (about 1000 patients) found 90-day mortality almost identical (about 43% in each arm) and was stopped for futility.

**ROSE controls had light sedation (ACURASYS controls were deeply sedated), and ROSE used higher PEEP; less proning in ROSE.** In ACURASYS, the comparison was paralysis vs deep sedation alone; in ROSE, it was paralysis with deep sedation vs light sedation, with a higher-PEEP strategy in both arms, which may itself reduce injurious effort.
mimic: Routine vs selective paralysis

Routine early paralysis is not supported after ROSE (ESICM 2023 recommends against routine continuous infusion); short paralysis is used for severe dyssynchrony despite deep sedation, during proning, or when plateau pressure cannot be controlled. The 2024 ATS update suggests it in early severe ARDS.
traps: “Early neuromuscular blockade helps every ARDS patient” (77% of the cohort got this right)
Against low tidal volume, higher PEEP and prone, early routine NMB is the one with no consistent benefit after ROSE.
“Use NMB indefinitely” or “no role of NMB” for persistent dyssynchrony despite deep sedation
Use it for a short period, about 24–48 h (NEET 2025).
decode: Atypical pneumonia → ARDS: which intervention is least likely to help? [DocT GT]
Early neuromuscular blockade.
Persistent dyssynchrony despite deep sedation — NMB, and for how long? [NEET 2025]
Yes, short duration (about 24–48 h).
ARDS-38.punch: ACURASYS (paralysis vs deep sedation) suggested benefit, ROSE (vs light sedation, higher PEEP) found none, so paralysis is now for 24–48 h in selected patients — dyssynchrony, proning, uncontrolled plateau pressure.

ARDS-39.intro: A leaky lung floods more when filling pressures are high, so less fluid should mean less oedema. FACTT tested that, but only once the patient was out of shock — the condition the question stem always hides in the wording.
why: **Conservative (CVP <4 or PAOP <8) vs liberal (CVP 10–14 or PAOP 14–18) fluid strategy over 7 days (1000 patients).** The conservative arm used diuretics and fluid restriction guided by filling pressures, urine output and perfusion — and only in patients who were no longer in shock.
**–136 mL vs +6992 mL.** The cumulative 7-day balance: roughly even with the conservative strategy, about 7 L positive with the liberal one.
**Ventilator-free days 14.6 vs 12.1, more ICU-free days, no increase in shock or dialysis.** Less lung water meant better oxygenation and earlier extubation, without harming the kidneys.

**Pulmonary artery catheter vs central venous catheter: no difference (27.4% vs 26.3%), more catheter complications with the PA catheter.** The paired catheter comparison showed a PA catheter added nothing but complications, mainly arrhythmias.
mimic: Resuscitation vs de-resuscitation
Fluids for shock come first; FACTT’s conservative strategy applies after shock has resolved.
traps: “Conservative fluids reduced mortality”
Not significant (25.5% vs 28.4%); the gain was ventilator-free days.
“Routine pulmonary artery catheter-guided resuscitation”
FACTT’s catheter comparison found no benefit and more complications.
decode: Haemodynamically stable ARDS — which fluid strategy improves oxygenation and ventilator-free days without more organ failure? [DocT GT]
Conservative fluid strategy after shock resolves.
[pattern] FACTT outcome
More ventilator-free days; no mortality difference.
ARDS-39.punch: FACTT: once shock has resolved, a conservative fluid strategy (balance about zero vs +7 L) gives more ventilator-free days without more renal failure, but no significant fall in mortality; the PA catheter adds only complications.

ARDS-40.intro: Steroids aim at the inflammation and the fibroproliferation that follows. The trials say that timing decides everything: started early they may help, started late they harm.
why: **Early low-dose methylprednisolone: ICU mortality 21% vs 43%.** Meduri’s trial (2007) gave methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/day within 72 h of onset; it was small (91 patients), so it was suggestive, not decisive.

**180 patients, persistent ARDS (day 7–28), methylprednisolone: no difference in 60- or 180-day mortality; more neuromyopathy.** LaSRS (ARDS Network) did improve oxygenation, compliance and blood pressure, and gave more ventilator-free and shock-free days at day 28 — but some patients needed re-intubation, and survival did not improve.

**Dexamethasone 20 mg for 5 days then 10 mg for 5 days: 60-day mortality 15.3% lower, more ventilator-free days.** DEXA-ARDS (2020) enrolled moderate-to-severe ARDS (P/F ≤200 on PEEP ≥10); mortality was about 21% vs 36%. It was stopped early for slow recruitment and was not blinded.
**Dexamethasone 6 mg in COVID-19 needing oxygen: lower mortality.** RECOVERY: the largest benefit was in ventilated patients, and none in patients not on oxygen (RESP01A, ARDS-12).

**Do not start 14 or more days after onset: LaSRS 60-day mortality 35% vs 8%; 180-day 44% vs 12%.** In the LaSRS subgroup started on day 14 or later, mortality was higher with steroids. The 2024 ATS update and the 2024 SCCM guideline now conditionally recommend corticosteroids in ARDS, on the evidence of trials that started them early.
mimic: Better physiology vs better survival
LaSRS improved oxygenation, compliance and shock-free days without saving lives — the questions test which outcome changed.
traps: “Late steroids (more than 2 weeks after onset) are beneficial”
They increased mortality in LaSRS.
“LaSRS: increased long-term survival”, “reduced weakness” or “no change in oxygenation” (only 59% chose more ventilator- and shock-free days)
LaSRS improved oxygenation and gave more ventilator- and shock-free days, with no survival benefit and more neuromuscular weakness.
“Corticosteroids should be started immediately” or “are contraindicated in all ARDS” (69% chose the keyed answer)
The keyed truth is that they improve oxygenation and respiratory compliance in early ARDS.
“Hypoglycaemia” or “hyperkalaemia” as the steroid side effect to watch (only 60% chose myopathy)
Steroids cause hyperglycaemia and hypokalaemia, and lower the lymphocyte count; myopathy is the keyed side effect, and LaSRS showed more neuromyopathy.
decode: Persistent ARDS for 8 days, methylprednisolone — outcome consistent with the ARDS Network trial? [DocT GT]
More ventilator- and shock-free days.
Which statement about steroids in ARDS is true? [DocT]
They improve oxygenation and respiratory compliance in early ARDS.
ICU patient on hydrocortisone — side effect to monitor? [DocT]
Myopathy.
ARDS-40.punch: Steroids help early — Meduri, DEXA-ARDS, RECOVERY — and harm late: started 14 or more days after onset, LaSRS mortality was 35% vs 8% at 60 days.

When
Result

ARDS-41.intro: Feeding was tested in two ARDS Network trials: how much to give early, and whether anti-inflammatory supplements help. Both answers were no difference or worse.
why: **Trophic vs full enteral feeding for the first 6 days: no difference in ventilator-free days or mortality; less gastrointestinal intolerance with trophic feeds.** EDEN (about 1000 patients) gave trophic feeds at a low rate; patients did as well, with less vomiting and fewer high gastric residuals.

**No benefit; stopped for futility with a signal of harm.** OMEGA gave omega-3 fatty acids, γ-linolenic acid and antioxidants twice daily; it was stopped early, with fewer ventilator-free days and more diarrhoea in the supplement arm.
mimic: Trophic vs full feeding
Same outcomes; trophic is better tolerated.
traps: “Omega-3 supplements improve ARDS outcomes”
OMEGA was stopped for futility with a signal of harm.
decode: [pattern] EDEN trial result
Trophic feeding for 6 days: same ventilator-free days and mortality, less GI intolerance.
ARDS-41.punch: EDEN: trophic feeding for the first 6 days does as well as full feeding with less intolerance; OMEGA: anti-inflammatory supplements failed and may harm.

ARDS-42.intro: Almost every drug aimed at a single step in ARDS — surfactant, inflammation, oxidants, the epithelium — has failed in trials. The list is asked as ‘which is NOT effective’ or as an evidence grade.
why: **Exogenous surfactant (adults).** Surfactant works in premature infants, who lack it; in adult ARDS the problem is injury and inactivation, and replacement did not help.

**Beta-2 agonists: BALTI-2 (IV salbutamol, harm), ALTA (inhaled).** They speed alveolar fluid clearance in the laboratory; IV salbutamol increased mortality in BALTI-2 and inhaled albuterol was futile in ALTA.
**Statins: SAILS, HARP-2.** Rosuvastatin (SAILS) and simvastatin (HARP-2) did not improve outcomes.

**Ketoconazole, lisofylline, ibuprofen, IV prostaglandin E1; N-acetylcysteine, procysteine, glutamine and other antioxidants; neutrophil elastase inhibitor, activated protein C; keratinocyte growth factor (harm).** All anti-inflammatory, antioxidant or repair strategies with no survival benefit.

**Aspirin for prevention (LIPS-A); inhaled nitric oxide and HFOV (no survival benefit).** LIPS-A gave aspirin to at-risk patients and did not prevent ARDS; iNO (ARDS-37) and HFOV (ARDS-34) failed for survival.
mimic: Failed drugs vs steroids
Steroids are not on this list: early steroids are now conditionally recommended (ARDS-40).
traps: “Recruitment manoeuvres are a grade B recommendation”

In the Harrison table Marrow uses, they are grade C. Low tidal volume is A; conservative fluids, higher PEEP, prone and ECMO are B; NMB and iNO are C; HFOV and surfactant are D. That table also grades steroids D, which is dated (ARDS-40).
“Inhaled β-agonists speed recovery”
ALTA (inhaled) was futile and BALTI-2 (IV) harmful.
decode: ARDS therapies: which is NOT a class B recommendation? [Marrow]
Recruitment manoeuvres (grade C).
[pattern] Which therapy is ineffective in ARDS?
Surfactant, β-agonists, statins, antioxidants, iNO — pick from the list.
ARDS-42.punch: Surfactant, β-agonists, statins, antioxidants, aspirin, iNO and HFOV all failed; what reduces mortality is ventilation — low tidal volume and prone — with early steroids the one drug now gaining support.

ARDS-43.sub: Respiratory → ARDS → Complications and causes of death
ARDS-43.intro: The story now moves from treatment to outcome. Patients with ARDS are ventilated for long periods, so the complications are those of prolonged critical illness, and what kills them is rarely the hypoxaemia itself.
why: **About 60%.** Prolonged ventilation, an injured lung and sedation make VAP common; published series range from about 15% to 60% (most between a third and a half), so 60% is the upper end.

**About 25% (hypoxic vasoconstriction, microthrombi, high airway pressures).** Each raises pulmonary vascular resistance and loads the right ventricle; echo shows a dilated RV with septal flattening. Prone and limiting plateau pressure and PaCO₂ unload it (ARDS-31c).
**Multi-organ dysfunction / sepsis, not refractory hypoxaemia.** Only a minority die of hypoxaemia; most die of the sepsis, shock and organ failure that caused or followed the ARDS.
**Barotrauma, ICU-acquired weakness, delirium, DVT, stress-ulcer bleeding.** These are the complications of a long ICU stay, and weakness and delirium lead into the long-term outcome (ARDS-44).
mimic: Dying with ARDS vs of hypoxaemia
Patients die with ARDS, of multi-organ failure, more often than of hypoxaemia.
traps: “Refractory hypoxaemia is the commonest cause of death”
Multi-organ failure and sepsis are (ARDS-46f).
decode: [pattern] Commonest cause of death in ARDS
Multi-organ dysfunction / sepsis.
ARDS-43.punch: ARDS brings VAP, acute cor pulmonale in about a quarter and the complications of a long ICU stay, and most patients die of multi-organ failure and sepsis, not of hypoxaemia.

ARDS-44.intro: For survivors, the question is what is left after discharge. Herridge’s Toronto cohort followed them for five years and found the lungs largely recovered while the person did not.
why: **109 survivors, followed for 5 years.** Relatively young adults (median age in the mid-40s), so the lasting disability is largely attributable to the critical illness itself rather than to old age.
**Median 436 m, 76% of predicted.** Exercise capacity improved over the first years but never returned to normal.

**Lung volumes and spirometry return to near normal (diffusing capacity mildly low). Persisting: muscle weakness and exercise limitation, cognitive and psychological problems (depression, PTSD), reduced quality of life.** The limit on walking is muscle wasting and weakness from the ICU stay, not the lung.
mimic: Pulmonary vs extrapulmonary sequelae
Lung function near normal; muscle, cognition and mood remain impaired.
traps: “ARDS survivors are limited by pulmonary fibrosis”
The lasting disability is neuromuscular and neuropsychological.
decode: [pattern] Main cause of long-term disability after ARDS
Muscle weakness and neuropsychological problems, not lung function.
ARDS-44.punch: Five years after ARDS, the lungs are near normal but walking distance is 76% of predicted, because muscle weakness, cognitive and psychological problems persist.

ARDS-45.sub: Respiratory → ARDS → Trials at a glance
ARDS-45.intro: The deck’s trials in one table. The questions give the trial name and ask what was compared, or give the intervention and ask which trial or what verdict.
why: **ARMA: 6 vs 12 mL/kg — mortality ↓.** 6 mL/kg predicted body weight with plateau ≤30 vs 12 mL/kg; mortality 31% vs 40%. This is the therapy best shown to improve survival.
**PROSEVA: prone ≥16 h — mortality ↓.** 16.0% vs 32.8% at 28 days (ARDS-30).
**ACURASYS: cisatracurium 48 h — benefit. ROSE: cisatracurium 48 h — no difference.** The difference lies in the control arms (ARDS-38).
**FACTT: conservative fluids — more ventilator-free days only.** No significant mortality difference (ARDS-39).
**OSCILLATE: HFOV — mortality ↑. ART: recruitment + high PEEP — mortality ↑.** Both opened the lung with high pressure (ARDS-33, 34).
**EOLIA: early VV-ECMO — not significant.** 35% vs 46%, P = 0.09 (ARDS-36).
mimic: Predicted vs actual body weight
ARMA used predicted (ideal) body weight, calculated from height and sex — not actual weight.
traps: “Diuresis, inhaled vasodilator or recruitment with PEEP titration is best shown to improve survival”
Low tidal volume (6 mL/kg IBW) is; FACTT improved ventilator-free days only, iNO oxygenation only, and ART showed harm.
“ARMA compared 6 vs 8 mL/kg actual body weight”
6 vs 12 mL/kg predicted body weight.
decode: Influenza ARDS on VT 500 mL, FiO₂ 1.0, PEEP 5 — which therapy is best shown to improve survival? [DocT GT]
Tidal volume 6 mL/kg ideal body weight.
ARMA compared which tidal volumes? [DocT GT]
6 vs 12 mL/kg predicted body weight.
ARDS-45.punch: Mortality fell with ARMA and PROSEVA, rose with OSCILLATE and ART, and did not change significantly with ROSE, FACTT or EOLIA; ACURASYS’s benefit was not reproduced.

ARDS-46.sub: Respiratory → ARDS → Revision: true or false
ARDS-46.intro: A sweep through the deck. Each statement turns on one number or verdict from an earlier card.
why: **False — OSCAR showed no difference; OSCILLATE showed harm** (ARDS-34).
**False — EOLIA P = 0.09 (0.07 on the survival curve)** (ARDS-36).
**True — LaSRS: steroids started ≥14 days after onset, 60-day mortality 35% vs 8%** (ARDS-40).
**False — iNO improves oxygenation only, and transiently** (ARDS-37).
**False — multi-organ failure / sepsis is the commonest cause of death** (ARDS-43).
traps: “P/F <200 for prone”
<150 is the PROSEVA threshold; <200 is the moderate ARDS band.
decode: [pattern] Statements about the rescue trials
Only ARMA and PROSEVA cut mortality significantly; OSCILLATE and ART raised it.
ARDS-46.punch: Most errors here come from mixing up the two HFOV trials, calling EOLIA significant, and forgetting that late steroids and routine paralysis did not help.

spine: Prone: the proven rescue
Prone positioning for at least 16 h a day, started early when P/F is below 150, roughly halved mortality in PROSEVA because it spreads strain evenly through the lung, not because it raises the PaO₂.
Forcing the lung open failed
Recruitment manoeuvres and high-frequency oscillation both open the lung with high pressure, and in ART and OSCILLATE that pressure cost lives, while OSCAR showed no gain.
ECMO and inhaled vasodilators
When protective ventilation and prone have failed, VV-ECMO is the rescue for set EOLIA thresholds, while inhaled vasodilators improve oxygenation for a day or two without improving survival.
Drugs, fluids and feeding
Paralysis, conservative fluids after shock and early steroids shorten ventilation more reliably than they save lives, late steroids harm, and almost every other drug tested has failed.
How patients die and recover
Most patients die of sepsis and multi-organ failure rather than hypoxaemia, and survivors’ lasting disability is in muscle and mind, not in the lung.
Trials at a glance
Each landmark trial is asked as a one-line verdict: which arm, which outcome, and whether it was significant.
RESP01C.primer: This deck assumes the basic lung-protective strategy is already running: tidal volume 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, plateau pressure ≤30 cmH₂O and adequate PEEP (ARDSNet, ARMA). Ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI) is damage done by the ventilator itself — over-stretching open alveoli (volutrauma), and repeated opening and closing of unstable ones (atelectrauma) — and most rescue therapies are judged by whether they reduce it. A therapy can improve PaO₂ without improving survival, so the questions always ask which outcome a trial changed: mortality, ventilator-free days, or only oxygenation. Ventilator-free days count the days alive and off the ventilator in the first 28, so they rise if patients either survive or come off the ventilator sooner.

COPD-01.intro: The deck starts with the lesion, because everything later — trapped air, intrinsic PEEP, hypercapnia — follows from it. COPD narrows the small airways and destroys the elastic tissue that normally pulls them open and pushes air out.
why: **Irreversible expiratory airflow limitation.** The limit is on expiration: inspiration is active and holds the airways open, whereas expiration relies on recoil and the airways narrow as the chest pressure rises. ‘Irreversible’ means not fully reversible with bronchodilators, which separates it from asthma (COPD-05).

**Raised resistance of small conducting airways (small-airway disease, chronic bronchitis), and raised lung compliance with loss of elastic recoil from emphysema.** Inflammation, mucus and fibrosis narrow the airway lumen. Emphysema removes the alveolar walls that tether small airways open, so they collapse during expiration, and removes the recoil that drives air out — the lung becomes easy to inflate (high compliance) but slow to empty.
**Peripheral airways below 2 mm diameter.** They contribute little to total resistance in health, so much of the disease is silent on simple tests until it is advanced.

**Smoke and pollutants → oxidative stress, neutrophil inflammation and inactivated anti-proteases → proteolytic destruction; alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is the genetic form.** Neutrophil elastase digests the alveolar wall and alpha-1 antitrypsin normally neutralises it; oxidants in smoke inactivate it. In the inherited deficiency the emphysema is panacinar, basal and early; in smokers it is centrilobular and upper-lobe.
mimic: Emphysema vs ARDS
Emphysema: compliance up, recoil down, slow emptying. ARDS: compliance down, fast emptying.
traps: “Lung compliance is reduced in emphysema” (COPD-14a)
It is increased: the elastic tissue is destroyed, so the lung inflates easily but recoils poorly.
decode: [pattern] Compliance and recoil in emphysema compared with fibrosis or ARDS
Emphysema raises compliance and lowers recoil; fibrosis and ARDS lower compliance.
COPD-01.punch: COPD is fixed expiratory airflow limitation from narrowed small airways (<2 mm) and emphysema; emphysema raises compliance and removes recoil, so the lung empties slowly.

COPD-02.intro: The slow-emptying lung of COPD-01 becomes dangerous when the next breath arrives too soon. Air left behind from each breath accumulates until the lung sits at a higher volume, and that trapped air explains intrinsic PEEP, the high work of breathing and the hypotension after intubation.
why: **The next breath starts before expiration is complete, so end-expiratory volume climbs above FRC with each breath (raised RV and FRC).** Normally expiration ends at the relaxed volume of the respiratory system. If flow is still going when inspiration begins, the leftover volume is added to the next breath; the volume climbs until the extra recoil at the higher volume pushes the tidal volume out in the time available, and the lung settles at that new, higher end-expiratory volume. On the ventilator, the flow–time trace shows expiratory flow that does not return to zero before the next breath.

**High expiratory resistance; short expiratory time; low elastic recoil; respiratory muscle dysfunction.** Resistance and low recoil slow the emptying; a fast rate, a long inspiration or a large tidal volume shortens the time allowed. A high minute ventilation (fever, acidosis, anxiety, over-ventilation by the clinician) is the commonest avoidable cause.

**Time constant = resistance × compliance; both are high in COPD, so emptying is slow.** One time constant empties about 63% of the volume, two about 86%, three about 95% — so roughly three are needed for near-complete emptying. Diseases with low compliance (ILD, ARDS) have short time constants and empty quickly, which is why auto-PEEP belongs to obstructive, not restrictive, disease.

**Intrinsic PEEP, higher elastic work of breathing, barotrauma, cardiovascular compromise, patient–ventilator dyssynchrony, misread pressures.** The trapped volume leaves alveolar pressure above zero at end-expiration (intrinsic PEEP, COPD-03); breathing at a high volume puts the muscles at a disadvantage and on the stiff upper part of the pressure–volume curve; high intrathoracic pressure cuts venous return (COPD-04) and is transmitted to the vessels, so CVP and pulmonary artery occlusion pressure read falsely high. Hypotension with a high wedge pressure can therefore come from trapped air, not a failing left ventricle.
mimic: Dynamic hyperinflation vs left-ventricular failure
Both raise the wedge pressure and lower blood pressure; with trapping the expiratory flow does not reach zero and a disconnection briefly restores the pressure.
traps: “Auto-PEEP results most commonly from distal airway obstruction in ILD or hypersensitivity pneumonitis” (65% right)
ILD lowers compliance and shortens the time constant, so the lung empties fast; auto-PEEP comes from high resistance and high compliance, as in COPD and asthma.
“Hypotension with raised PAOP in a ventilated COPD patient is LV failure”
Trapped air raises intrathoracic pressure, which lowers venous return and is transmitted into the PA catheter reading; the flow trace not returning to zero is the clue.
“Intubated asthmatic, pH 7.16, PaCO₂ 66: raise the rate to clear CO₂”

A faster rate shortens expiration and worsens trapping. Lower the rate, raise inspiratory flow and accept the hypercapnia. The keyed option’s phrase ‘metabolic compensation’ is wrong: a bicarbonate of 25 means an acute, uncompensated respiratory acidosis.
decode: Ventilated COPD, hypotension, raised PAOP, expiratory flow persisting into the next breath — mechanism? [DocT GT]
Dynamic hyperinflation.
All true about mechanical ventilation EXCEPT [DocT QBank]
The false one: auto-PEEP commonly from ILD. Peak pressure reflects resistance and compliance; plateau reflects compliance only.
Intubated asthmatic, worsening pH 7.16, PaCO₂ 66 — disorder and change? [Marrow]
Acute respiratory acidosis; lower the rate (to about 20) and increase inspiratory flow.
Why does auto-PEEP happen? [NEET 2024]
Incomplete exhalation because expiratory time is too short for the time constant.
COPD-02.punch: Dynamic hyperinflation is air that a slow-emptying lung (high resistance × high compliance) cannot get out before the next breath; the fix is more expiratory time — lower rate, faster inspiration, accept hypercapnia — never a faster rate.

Why it helps

the breath is delivered faster, leaving more time to exhale

COPD-03.sub: Respiratory → COPD → Intrinsic PEEP and the work of breathing
COPD-03.intro: Trapped air leaves a positive pressure in the alveoli at the end of expiration (COPD-02). This card asks what that pressure costs the patient with every breath, and the one question tests why adding external PEEP helps.
why: **The patient must first generate a negative pressure equal to intrinsic PEEP before any flow or trigger occurs: an inspiratory threshold load.** Flow into the lung needs alveolar pressure below the pressure at the airway opening. With PEEPi of 8, the muscles must lower alveolar pressure by 8 cmH₂O simply to reach zero flow, and only then can the ventilator sense the effort; much of the effort is wasted, and weak efforts fail to trigger at all. External PEEP set below PEEPi (commonly up to about 80% of it) raises the circuit pressure, so the gap the patient must overcome shrinks; because the narrowed airways limit flow, this does not add to the trapped volume as long as it stays below PEEPi.

**A larger pressure gradient is needed for a given flow (resistance); more dead space, so a higher minute volume is needed for a normal CO₂.** Emphysema creates ventilated but poorly perfused units, so a larger share of each breath is wasted, and the patient must breathe more to clear the same CO₂ — which shortens expiration and worsens the trapping.

**Flattened diaphragm and altered chest-wall geometry; resistive loads; hypoxaemia and acidosis impair muscle metabolism; cachexia; steroids and malnutrition.** A flattened diaphragm has short fibres and a large radius of curvature, so it generates little pressure for its tension. Supply is limited while demand is high, so fatigue and hypercapnia follow.
mimic: Ineffective triggering vs double triggering

Ineffective (missed) triggering comes from PEEPi: efforts appear as dips in the flow trace with no breath. Double triggering is two breaths for one effort, from an inspiratory time shorter than the patient’s.
traps: “External PEEP lengthens expiratory time”
It does not change expiratory time; it narrows the gap between alveolar and circuit pressure, lowering the threshold load.
“External PEEP increases the gradient between alveoli and circuit”
It reduces it; that is how it helps the patient trigger.
decode: AECOPD on BiPAP, distressed, failing to trigger — how does external PEEP reduce work of breathing? [DocT GT]
It reduces the threshold load imposed by PEEPi, so the patient’s effort reaches the trigger sooner.
COPD-03.punch: Intrinsic PEEP is a threshold the patient must pull through before every breath; external PEEP set just below it lowers that threshold without adding hyperinflation.

COPD-04.sub: Respiratory → COPD → Positive pressure and the circulation
COPD-04.intro: Trapped air already raises intrathoracic pressure (COPD-02); positive-pressure ventilation adds more. This card explains why the blood pressure falls, and the one question tests the same physiology in ARDS: what raises pulmonary vascular resistance.
why: **Raised intrathoracic pressure → less venous return (preload); hyperinflation compresses alveolar vessels and hypoxia constricts them → higher RV afterload.** Venous return depends on the gradient from the veins to the right atrium; raising pleural pressure narrows it. Pulmonary vascular resistance is lowest near FRC: above it, alveolar vessels are stretched and squeezed by the distended alveoli, so positive pressure on an over-inflated lung raises the resistance the right ventricle pumps against.

**RV dilates, septum shifts left (ventricular interdependence) → LV filling falls.** The two ventricles share a septum and the pericardium, so a distended right ventricle leaves less room for the left.

**Fall in blood pressure, worst just after intubation.** At that moment sedatives remove sympathetic tone, the patient is often dry after days of poor intake, and bagging is usually too fast, adding trapped air. If the pressure falls, disconnect the ventilator for 30–60 seconds: if it recovers as the chest empties, trapping was the cause; if not, think of tension pneumothorax.
mimic: Trapping vs tension pneumothorax after intubation
Both cause hypotension and high pressures; disconnection restores the blood pressure in trapping but not in a tension pneumothorax, which needs decompression.
traps: “Decreased alveolar pressure raises PVR”
Higher alveolar pressure compresses alveolar vessels and raises PVR; prostacyclin and systemic vasodilators lower it.
decode: Ventilated severe ARDS, new RV dysfunction, rising PA pressures with stable left-sided pressures — what raised PVR? [DocT GT]
Positive-pressure ventilation.
[pattern] COPD hypotensive minutes after intubation — first step?
Disconnect from the ventilator and let the chest empty; then slower rate, fluid.
COPD-04.punch: Positive pressure on a hyperinflated chest cuts venous return and squeezes the alveolar vessels, so the right ventricle fails to fill and to empty; when the pressure falls after intubation, disconnect first.

COPD-05.intro: The two obstructive diseases look alike at the bedside, but they differ in inflammation, reversibility and the way they fail. The questions test the last: an old smoker with hyperinflation and a high PaCO₂ has type 2 failure from COPD.
why: **Asthma: eosinophils, mast cells, T-lymphocytes; COPD: neutrophils, macrophages.** Asthma is driven by type 2 (Th2) inflammation, which is why it responds to steroids; COPD inflammation is neutrophilic and responds less. A raised blood eosinophil count in COPD marks those most likely to benefit from inhaled steroids: the benefit grows with the count and is clearest at ≥300/µL (COPD-07).

**Asthma reversible (becomes fixed with time); COPD irreversible.** Long-standing asthma remodels the airway and the obstruction can become fixed, so reversibility alone does not always separate them.
**Airway hyper-responsiveness, with mucosal oedema, mucus hypersecretion and wall thickening.** The airways narrow too much and too easily in response to triggers.

**Type 2 (hypercapnic).** V/Q mismatch with a large dead space, a high CO₂ load and tiring muscles cannot be matched by ventilation, so PaCO₂ rises. Acute asthma, by contrast, usually starts with a low PaCO₂ from hyperventilation (COPD-08).
mimic: Acute asthma vs AECOPD on the gas
Asthma: low PaCO₂ early, so a normal value is ominous. COPD: often a high PaCO₂, and the pH says whether it is acute.
traps: “PaO₂ 55, PaCO₂ 70 with hyperinflation is type 1 failure or acute asthma” (89% right)
A raised PaCO₂ defines type 2; a 72-year-old smoker with flat diaphragms points to COPD.
“In mild asthma, submucosal mast cells are fewer and mainly tryptase–chymase type” (87% right)
That pattern belongs to severe asthma; mild asthma keeps tryptase-only mast cells, as in normal lung.
decode: Smoker, RR 36, cyanosed, PaO₂ 55, PaCO₂ 70, hyperinflated chest X-ray — diagnosis? [DocT QBank]
Type 2 respiratory failure due to COPD.
All true about asthma pathology EXCEPT [DocT GT]
The statement placing reduced, tryptase–chymase mast cells in mild asthma.
COPD-05.punch: Asthma is eosinophilic, reversible and hyper-responsive; COPD is neutrophilic and fixed, and its exacerbations fail as type 2 (hypercapnic) failure.

COPD-06.intro: An exacerbation is what brings the COPD patient to the ICU. The card defines it and lists its cause and severity signs; the questions test how often bacteria are found and which single sign marks a severe attack.
why: **Worsening of respiratory symptoms that leads to a change in medication.** This is the older operational GOLD wording. Since 2023 GOLD uses the Rome definition: dyspnoea and/or cough and sputum that worsen over 14 days or less, often with tachypnoea or tachycardia, caused by infection, pollution or another insult.

**Increased dyspnoea, increased sputum volume, increased sputum purulence (Anthonisen).** All three make a type 1 exacerbation; Anthonisen found antibiotics helped most when purulence was present. GOLD suggests antibiotics when purulence is accompanied by more dyspnoea or more sputum, or when the patient needs ventilation.

**Infection: respiratory viruses; Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis.** Rhinovirus is the commonest virus. Bacteria are found in the lower airways in about half of exacerbations, but many patients are colonised when stable, so a positive sputum does not prove a bacterial cause. Pseudomonas appears in very severe disease.

**Accessory muscle use, paradoxical chest-wall movement, new or worse central cyanosis, peripheral oedema, haemodynamic instability, altered mental status.** Altered mental status is the most important single sign: it means CO₂ narcosis or exhaustion, so the patient needs a blood gas, escalation and readiness to intubate (COPD-10, COPD-12).
mimic: Exacerbation vs pneumonia, pulmonary embolism or heart failure
These cause or mimic exacerbations and are looked for in every admission; a new infiltrate makes it pneumonia.
traps: “Sputum colour grades severity”
Purulence suggests bacteria and guides antibiotics; severity is graded by effort, mental state, haemodynamics and the gas.
“Bacteria in sputum prove a bacterial exacerbation”
Colonisation is common; about half of exacerbations have lower-airway bacteria.
decode: Share of AECOPD with organisms in the lower airways [Marrow]
About 50%.
Most important sign of a severe COPD exacerbation [Marrow]
Change in mental status.
COPD-06.punch: An exacerbation is a short-term worsening of dyspnoea, sputum and purulence, mostly infective; altered mental status is the sign that it is severe.

COPD-07.intro: Spirometry makes the diagnosis and grades airflow limitation, but the grade does not choose the treatment. The questions test the cut-offs, the obstructive pattern and the ABE groups that decide discharge inhalers.
why: **Post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC <0.7.** The ratio, not FEV₁, diagnoses obstruction; post-bronchodilator values remove the reversible part, so a low ratio that persists is fixed limitation. ILD and other restrictive diseases reduce both volumes and keep the ratio normal or high.
**GOLD 1 mild ≥80; 2 moderate 50–79; 3 severe 30–49; 4 very severe <30 (FEV₁ % predicted).** Each boundary value belongs to the milder grade: FEV₁ of exactly 50% is GOLD 2, and exactly 30% is GOLD 3.
mimic: GOLD grade vs ABE group
The grade (1–4) describes airflow; the group (A, B, E) comes from symptoms and exacerbations and chooses therapy.
traps: “FEV₁ 50% is GOLD 3” (only 64% right)
GOLD 3 is 30–49%; 50% is the bottom of GOLD 2.
“Discharge after an admitted exacerbation on salbutamol alone, or straight to triple therapy” (only 40% right)
One hospitalised exacerbation puts him in group E: LABA + LAMA. Inhaled steroid is added only if eosinophils are ≥300/µL, because it raises pneumonia risk.
“Low FEV₁ with low ratio is ILD or restriction”
A low ratio is obstruction; restriction keeps the ratio normal or high.
decode: FEV₁/FVC <0.7, FEV₁ 50% predicted — GOLD grade? [DocT QBank]
GOLD 2.
Admitted COPD exacerbation — discharge inhalers? [DocT QBank]
LABA + LAMA (formoterol plus tiotropium).
Low FEV₁, FEV₁/FVC <0.7 — diagnosis? [NEET 2025]
COPD.
COPD-07.punch: A post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC below 0.7 diagnoses COPD and FEV₁ grades it (≥80, 50–79, 30–49, <30), but exacerbation history and symptoms (group E) choose LABA + LAMA at discharge.

COPD-08.intro: Severity in asthma is judged at the bedside and confirmed by peak flow and the gas. The six questions turn on one point above all: a breathless asthmatic should have a low PaCO₂, so a normal one means he is tiring.
why: **Cannot complete a sentence in one breath; accessory muscle use; RR >30; HR >120; pulsus paradoxus; no response to treatment.** These are the GINA-style severe features. Pulsus paradoxus comes from large negative swings in pleural pressure that pool blood in the lungs and shift the septum on inspiration, so it is present while the patient can still generate effort (COPD-09).
**PEFR ≤50% of predicted.** Peak flow is the objective measure of airflow; it is checked again after treatment.

**PaO₂ <60 mmHg (8 kPa) on air; PaCO₂ >45 mmHg (6 kPa).** Early in an attack the drive to breathe is high and PaCO₂ is low. A PaCO₂ that rises to normal (about 40–45) means ventilation can no longer keep up — the muscles are failing. Grading differs by guideline: BTS calls a normal PaCO₂ ‘life-threatening’ and a raised one ‘near-fatal’.
mimic: Normal PaCO₂ in asthma vs in COPD
In asthma it marks fatigue; in COPD a high PaCO₂ may be chronic, and the pH decides.
traps: “PaCO₂ 42 after bronchodilators means a successful response or is normal” (only 41% right)
In acute asthma PaCO₂ should be low; normal means impending respiratory failure.
“PaCO₂ 42, pH 7.35 means asthma with normal ventilation” (74% right)
Same point: in a breathless asthmatic who cannot speak, a normal PaCO₂ is the warning.
“PEF 68% after 2 h in the ED: discharge”

That is short of the usual emergency-department discharge bar, a PEF above 70% sustained for an hour after the last bronchodilator; and patients discharged after less than about 2 hours of treatment relapse often. Observe and recheck.
decode: Acute asthma, PaCO₂ 42 after bronchodilators — implication? [DocT GT, two tests]
Impending respiratory failure.
Severe wheeze, cannot speak, RR 28, PaCO₂ 42, pH 7.35 [DocT QBank]
Asthma exacerbation with impending respiratory failure.
Which finding marks life-threatening asthma? [Marrow]
PaO₂ 7.7 kPa (below 8 kPa).
ED asthma, PEF 68% after 2 h — disposition? [Marrow]
Observe for 2 more hours and recheck PEF and symptoms.
COPD-08.punch: Severe asthma is RR >30, HR >120, PEF ≤50%, and words not sentences; in that patient a PaCO₂ that is ‘normal’ means he is tiring and about to fail.
